name: Ben Nevis
description: Ben Nevis mountain is 1,345 metres (4,413 feet) tall — the highest mountain in the UK and the British Isles. Located in Lochaber, Highland, Scotland near Fort William, it attracts 130,000–150,000 walkers each year and is the most climbed peak in the country.
history: The first recorded ascent was in 1771 by botanist James Robertson. The mountain's name comes from the Gaelic "Beinn Nibheis" meaning "malicious mountain" or "mountain with its head in the clouds". A meteorological observatory operated on the summit from 1883 to 1904.

The summit plateau is the collapsed dome of an ancient volcano — Ben Nevis is a volcanic mountain
Snow can remain on the mountain year-round in sheltered gullies on the north face
The first timed race up Ben Nevis was in 1895, and the men's course record of 1hr 25min 34sec, set by Kenny Stuart in 1984, still stands

The summit hosted a continuously staffed weather observatory from 1883 to 1904 — its ruins remain today
Ben Nevis is classified as both a Munro and a Marilyn, reflecting its height and prominence
famous_for: being the highest mountain in the UK
walking_guide: The Ben Nevis Mountain Track (also called the Pony Track or Tourist Path) is the route most visitors take to the summit of Ben Nevis, the highest mountain in the UK. It begins at the Glen Nevis visitor centre car park (postcode PH33 6ST) and follows a clear stone path up the western slopes, passing the Halfway Lochan and the old observatory ruins before reaching the 1,345m summit cairn. The round trip is approximately 10.5 miles (17km) with roughly 1,350m of ascent, and takes 7–9 hours for a fit walker. The path is well-built but relentless — about 1,350m of ascent over 8.5km each way. In summer the Ben Nevis Mountain Track is straightforward underfoot, but the summit plateau is notoriously featureless and dangerous in poor visibility: always carry a map and compass, and know how to take a bearing. OS Explorer 392 (Ben Nevis & Fort William) is the recommended Ben Nevis route map. The alternative CMD Arete route approaches from the north-east via the Carn Mor Dearg ridge and is one of the finest moderate scrambles in Scotland — grade 2-3 in summer conditions, but a serious winter climb from November to March. For the full experience, acclimatise in Glen Nevis the day before, start early to avoid afternoon clouds on the summit, and check the Met Office mountain forecast before setting out. A Ben Nevis tourist path map is available at the visitor centre.

faqs.answer: May to September offers the most stable conditions, longest daylight, and snow-free paths on the standard Mountain Track. From November to March, Ben Nevis is a genuine winter mountaineering objective requiring ice axe, crampons, and winter skills.

seo_title: Ben Nevis Mountain: Height, Routes & Complete Guide
seo_description: Ben Nevis mountain is the UK's highest peak at 1,345m (4,413ft). How high is Ben Nevis in metres? Discover its routes, maps, and climbing facts.
seo_h1: Ben Nevis Mountain: The UK's Highest Peak
seo_key_takeaways: Ben Nevis mountain is 1,345 metres (4,413 feet) high — the highest mountain in the UK, Scotland, and the British Isles. [Source: Ordnance Survey]
It sits in the Grampian Mountains near Fort William in Lochaber, Highland, Scotland — postcode PH33 6ST for the Glen Nevis car park.
The Ben Nevis Mountain Track (also called the Pony Track or Tourist Path) is the standard route: ~17km round trip, 7–9 hours, roughly 1,350m of ascent.
It forms part of the National Three Peaks Challenge alongside Snowdon (1,085m) and Scafell Pike (978m), and is 36m taller than the UK's second-highest peak, Ben Macdui (1,309m).
about_extra:
Ben Nevis mountain draws over 150,000 walkers a year, more than any other Scottish mountain, which makes route choice and timing more important here than on quieter peaks — the Ben Nevis Mountain Track can be genuinely congested on a clear summer weekend. In practice, the busiest window is 10am–2pm on the lower half of the Mountain Track; setting off before 8am avoids most of the crowding and gives more daylight buffer for the descent.

Underestimating the summit plateau in poor visibility is a common mistake — the flat, featureless top has claimed lives from walkers who wandered off-path near Five Finger Gully in cloud. Even on the "Moderate" tourist route, a map, compass (or reliable GPS), and the confidence to use them are not optional extras.

What type of mountain is Ben Nevis? Geologically, the summit sits on the collapsed dome of an ancient Devonian volcano. The dramatic north face cliffs — up to 600m high — are the eroded remains of that volcanic structure, making Ben Nevis a volcanic mountain rather than a folded sedimentary peak. This geology also explains why the north face is one of the most important winter climbing venues in the UK, with classic routes like Point Five Gully and Zero Gully attracting climbers from across the world.

Ben Nevis is sometimes confused with Ben Wyvis, a separate 1,046m mountain in the northern Highlands near Dingwall. The two are entirely different peaks — Ben Wyvis is a Munro about 63 miles (100km) north-north-east of Ben Nevis, while mountain Ben Nevis is the UK's highest summit at 1,345m in Lochaber. If you're planning a trip, make sure your map, accommodation and route guide refer to the right one.

Ben Nevis is 1,345 metres (4,413 feet) above sea level, according to Ordnance Survey data confirmed in 2016. This makes it the highest mountain in Scotland, the UK, and the British Isles. In Ben Nevis metres, the figure is 1,345m; in feet, 4,413ft — roughly 260m taller than Snowdon, the tallest peak in Wales. extra_sections.title: Where Is Ben Nevis?
extra_sections.body:
Ben Nevis is in Lochaber, Highland, Scotland, close to the town of Fort William. What country is Ben Nevis in? It is in Scotland, within the United Kingdom. The mountain sits at the western end of the Grampian Mountains, overlooking Glen Nevis to the south and Loch Eil to the north.

The OS grid reference for the summit is NN 166 712. The nearest town is Fort William, about 4 miles (7km) from the summit in a straight line, which serves as the main base for walkers climbing Ben Nevis. Fort William has a railway station, bus connections, and a full range of accommodation. The parking postcode for the Glen Nevis visitor centre car park is PH33 6ST.

Ben Nevis is within the Lochaber Geopark, a UNESCO-recognised area of outstanding geological interest. The mountain's dramatic north face — with cliffs up to 600m high — is visible from Fort William and is one of the most iconic mountain landscapes in Scotland.

extra_sections.title: What Mountain Range Is Ben Nevis In?
extra_sections.body:
Ben Nevis is part of the Grampian Mountains, the largest mountain range in Scotland. The Grampians stretch from the southwest Highlands through the central Highlands to the Cairngorms in the east, and include most of Scotland's highest peaks.

The Ben Nevis range of mountains specifically refers to a small cluster of peaks around Ben Nevis itself, including Carn Mor Dearg (1,220m), Carn Dearg Meadhonach (1,181m), and Aonach Beag (1,234m). These peaks form a horseshoe ridge around the north face of Ben Nevis, and the CMD Arete route connecting Carn Mor Dearg to Ben Nevis is widely regarded as one of the finest ridge walks in the UK.

So if you're asking which mountain range Ben Nevis is in, the answer is the Grampian Mountains — a broad range that also encompasses the Cairngorms, where Ben Macdui (1,309m) and Braeriach (1,296m), the UK's second and third highest peaks, are found.

extra_sections.title: Ben Nevis Routes and Track Map
extra_sections.body: There are two main Ben Nevis hiking routes that walkers use to reach the summit: 1. The Ben Nevis Mountain Track (Pony Track / Tourist Path) — the standard route for most walkers. It starts at the Glen Nevis visitor centre car park (postcode PH33 6ST), follows a well-built stone path up the western side of the mountain, and reaches the summit via the Halfway Lochan and the old observatory ruins. The round trip is about 10.5 miles (17km) with roughly 1,350m of ascent, taking 7–9 hours for a fit walker. A Ben Nevis tourist path map is available at the visitor centre, and OS Explorer 392 covers the route in detail. 2. The CMD Arete (Carn Mor Dearg Arete) — a spectacular ridge walk approaching Ben Nevis from the north-east. It begins from the North Face car park, ascends Carn Mor Dearg (1,220m), and follows a narrow rocky arete to the summit of Ben Nevis. This route is longer and more exposed, requiring scrambling skills and a head for heights. It is one of the finest moderate mountain routes in Scotland. For a Ben Nevis routes map, we recommend carrying OS Explorer 392 (Ben Nevis & Fort William) or Harvey's Ben Nevis Superwalker map. Both show the Mountain Track, CMD Arete, and the surrounding peaks in clear detail. Always check the Met Office mountain forecast before setting out, and carry a Ben Nevis route map even on clear days — the summit plateau is notoriously featureless in cloud.

extra_sections.title: Is Ben Nevis a Mountain?
extra_sections.body:
Yes — Ben Nevis is unquestionably a mountain. At 1,345m (4,413ft) it far exceeds the 600m (2,000ft) threshold commonly used to distinguish mountains from hills in the UK, and it is classified as both a Munro (a Scottish peak over 3,000ft / 914m) and a Marilyn (a peak with 150m+ of topographic prominence).

What type of mountain is Ben Nevis? Geologically, Ben Nevis is the remains of an ancient volcano. The summit sits on the collapsed inner dome of a Devonian volcanic centre, and the dramatic north face cliffs are the eroded remains of the volcanic structure. This makes Ben Nevis a volcanic mountain, distinct from the folded sedimentary mountains found in parts of the Lake District and Wales.

The mountain is named from the Gaelic "Beinn Nibheis", often translated as "malicious mountain" or "mountain with its head in the clouds" — a fitting description given how frequently the summit is shrouded in mist.

extra_sections.title: Best Time to Climb Ben Nevis, Month by Month
extra_sections.body: May–September: most stable window, longest daylight, both routes at their stated grade without winter skills required. October & April: shoulder season — expect some snow on the summit plateau even in a mild year; check current conditions before relying on the standard grade. November–March: a genuine winter mountaineering objective. The CMD Arete in particular becomes a Grade I/II winter climb requiring ice axe, crampons, and the experience to use them.

extra_sections.title: Ben Nevis vs. Ben Wyvis — Quick Clarification
extra_sections.body: Ben Nevis and Ben Wyvis are two entirely different mountains. Ben Nevis (1,345m) is the UK's highest peak, near Fort William in the Lochaber Geopark. Ben Wyvis (1,046m) is a separate Munro about 63 miles (100km) north-north-east, near Dingwall in Easter Ross, known for its long whaleback ridge rather than any connection to Ben Nevis.

name: Ben Macdui
description: Ben Macdui is the second highest mountain in the British Isles and the highest in the Cairngorms. At 1,309 meters, it offers spectacular views across the Cairngorm plateau.
history: The mountain is named after the Clan MacDuff. For many years, it was thought to be higher than Ben Nevis. The summit is home to legends of the "Big Grey Man" or "Fear Liath Mòr", a supernatural presence said to haunt the mountain.
fun_facts: Second highest mountain in Britain
Home to the legend of the Big Grey Man
Part of the Cairngorms plateau
Often climbed from Cairn Gorm ski area
Has a large summit cairn
walking_guide:
Ben Macdui is usually climbed from the Cairngorm ski area car park, following a path across the high plateau. The ascent is long and the terrain is open and stony, so the round trip takes six to eight hours. A longer approach from Glen Derry or Glenmore gives a more remote feel.

The summit plateau is vast, windy and cold, even in summer, and navigation is very difficult in mist. A viewpoint indicator on the summit, installed in the 1920s, names the surrounding hills. The mountain is associated with the legend of the Grey Man of Ben Macdui, a ghostly presence said to haunt the summit, which adds to its atmosphere.

name: Braeriach
description: Braeriach is the third highest mountain in the UK and the highest point in the western Cairngorms. Its vast summit plateau is home to arctic-alpine flora and one of Scotland's few permanent snowbeds.
history: Braeriach's vast summit plateau holds the Wells of Dee, the source of the River Dee, which rise at one of the highest altitudes of any river source in Britain. Its northern corrie, Garbh Choire Mor, holds snow for much of the year and sometimes through the summer.
fun_facts: Braeriach is the third highest mountain in Britain
The River Dee rises at the Wells of Dee on the plateau
Garbh Choire Mor holds snow late into the summer
The Lairig Ghru pass runs beneath its eastern flank
Cairn Toul and the Angel's Peak lie across the Garbh Choire
walking_guide:
Braeriach is a committing day. Most walkers approach from the Cairngorm side through Chalamain Gap and the Lairig Ghru, then climb onto the plateau by the Sron na Lairige ridge. Allow at least nine to eleven hours for the round trip, and more if you add the neighbouring tops.

The plateau is high, open and very exposed, and the weather can be severe even in summer. Navigation in mist is hard, so you need a map and compass and the skill to use them. The reward is one of the finest views in Britain, down into the Garbh Choire and across to Cairn Toul.

name: Cairn Toul
description: Cairn Toul is the fourth highest mountain in Scotland, connected to Braeriach by a high col. The mountain offers spectacular views over the Lairig Ghru.
history: Cairn Toul sits across the Lairig Ghru from Ben Macdui and above the Devil's Point, a rocky tower at the head of Glen Dee. The mountain forms a pair with the Angel's Peak, Sgor an Lochain Uaine, and the two are often climbed together.
fun_facts: Cairn Toul is the fourth highest mountain in Britain
The Devil's Point rises at the foot of the mountain beside Corrour Bothy
Sgor an Lochain Uaine, the Angel's Peak, lies on the same ridge
The Lairig Ghru passes beneath it
Corrour Bothy, a famous mountain shelter, sits in the glen
walking_guide:
Cairn Toul is reached either from Linn of Dee through Glen Dee and past Corrour Bothy, or from the Cairngorm side through the Lairig Ghru. Both approaches are long. Allow ten hours or more, and consider cycling the track to save time. Many walkers combine Cairn Toul with the Angel's Peak and Braeriach for a major day.

The terrain is rough and the plateau exposed, and mobile signal is non-existent. This is a mountain for experienced walkers who are happy with long days and navigation in poor visibility. Check the stalking information and tell someone your route.

name: Sgor an Lochain Uaine
description: Also known as the Angel's Peak, this Munro is famous for its green lochan and dramatic cliffs. It's often climbed as part of a Cairngorms plateau traverse.

name: Cairn Gorm
description: Cairn Gorm (1,245m) is one of the best-known summits in the Cairngorms National Park, home to the UK's highest funicular railway and a busy ski centre. Despite its fame, Cairn Gorm is not the highest peak in the Cairngorms — that title belongs to Ben Macdui (1,309m), the second-highest mountain in the UK, which sits roughly 5 km to the south-west. Cairn Gorm is, however, the sixth-highest mountain in the UK and a popular day out for hillwalkers, skiers, and winter climbers alike.
history: The name means "Blue Hill" in Gaelic, referring to the blue-grey granite that forms the mountain. A ski resort has operated on its slopes since the 1960s, and the funicular railway opened in 2001.
fun_facts: Gave its name to the Cairngorms range
Home to Scotland's only funicular railway
Popular ski resort in winter
Summit plateau is arctic-alpine environment
One of five Scottish 4000-foot mountains
famous_for: its funicular railway and winter ski resort
walking_guide: The most popular route to the summit of Cairn Gorm starts from the Coire Cas car park at the foot of the ski area, near Aviemore. The path climbs north-west through the ski developments, passing the Ptarmigan Station at 1,097m before continuing to the true summit at 1,245m - a round trip of roughly 8 km taking 3-4 hours for fit walkers. For a quieter and more scenic approach, the Windy Ridge Path follows the north-western ridge from the same car park, avoiding the ski infrastructure and offering fine views across the Cairngorm Plateau. In winter, Cairn Gorm becomes Scotland's busiest ski resort with 22 runs served by the funicular and chairlifts, and the northern corries - particularly Coire an t-Sneachda and Coire Domhain - are renowned for ice and mixed climbing from December to March. The summit sits on the edge of the Cairngorm Plateau, a vast arctic-alpine landscape and one of the wildest areas in the British Isles; navigation can be challenging in poor visibility, so always carry a map and compass. Check the Mountain Weather Information Service forecast before setting out, as the plateau can be dangerously icy in winter and surprisingly cold even in midsummer.

faqs.question: How high is Cairngorm mountain?
faqs.answer: Cairn Gorm stands at 1,245m (4,085 ft) at its summit, making it the sixth-highest mountain in Scotland.

faqs.question: Is Cairn Gorm the same as the Cairngorms?
faqs.answer: No. Cairn Gorm is one mountain; the Cairngorms is the wider range of peaks — including Ben Macdui, Braeriach and Cairn Toul — that takes its name from Cairn Gorm.

faqs.question: Which is the highest mountain in the Cairngorms National Park?
faqs.answer: Ben Macdui, at 1,309m — not Cairn Gorm. Despite giving its name to the range, Cairn Gorm is only the fourth-highest summit in the Cairngorms.

faqs.question: Can I get to the Cairn Gorm summit by funicular?
faqs.answer: The funicular takes you as far as the Ptarmigan Station (1,097m), leaving a short walk to the true summit — it doesn't run directly to the top. The railway has also had repeated multi-month and multi-year closures for structural repairs since 2018, so check Cairngorm Mountain's live status before basing a visit around it; the walking routes are unaffected by funicular closures.

seo_title: Cairngorm Mountain Height: Summit Facts & Figures
seo_description: Cairngorm mountain height stands at 1,245m, Scotland's 6th-highest peak. Learn why Ben Macdui actually outranks it in the Cairngorms, plus routes.
seo_h1: Cairngorm Mountain Height: Facts About Cairn Gorm's Summit
seo_key_takeaways: Cairngorm mountain height is 1,245m (4,085 ft), Scotland's 6th-highest peak.
Despite giving its name to the whole Cairngorms range, Cairn Gorm is not the highest mountain in the Cairngorms — that title belongs to Ben Macdui at 1,309m.
Home to the Cairngorm Mountain ski resort and a funicular railway.
Recorded the UK's highest-ever official wind gust: 173mph in 1986.
about_extra: Cairn Gorm rises dramatically above Aviemore and the Strathspey valley, its northern flanks carved into a series of corries that hold snow well into spring. The mountain's funicular railway, opened in 2001, runs from the Base Station at 637m to the Ptarmigan Station at 1,097m, giving visitors a taste of the high plateau without the climb — though walkers heading for the true summit still need to complete the final 150m on foot. The summit of Cairn Gorm sits on the western edge of the Cairngorm Plateau, a vast arctic-alpine landscape that is one of the wildest areas in the British Isles. The plateau is home to rare wildlife including ptarmigan, mountain hare, and the UK's only herd of reindeer, reintroduced in 1952. The plateau's sheer size means navigation can be challenging in poor visibility, and walkers should carry a map and compass even on seemingly straightforward summer days. It is a common misconception that Cairn Gorm is the highest mountain in the Cairngorms. That distinction belongs to Ben Macdui (1,309m), the second-highest mountain in the UK, approximately 5 km south-west of Cairn Gorm's summit. The Cairngorm range also contains Braeriach (1,296m), Cairn Toul (1,291m), and Sgor an Lochain Uaine (1,258m), all of which are higher than or comparable to Cairn Gorm itself. The range gets its name from An Càrn Gorm ('the blue-grey hill' in Gaelic), referring specifically to this peak. In winter, Cairn Gorm is Scotland's busiest ski resort, with 22 runs and a vertical drop of 470m served by the funicular and several chairlifts. The Coire na Sgreuchaill and Coire Cas areas offer the most reliable snow, though conditions vary enormously from year to year. Winter climbers also flock to the northern corries — particularly Coire an t-Sneachda and Coire Domhain — for ice and mixed routes that form reliably from December to March. For summer walkers, the most popular route to the summit starts from the Coire Cas car park and follows the path through the ski area to the top, a round trip of roughly 8 km taking 3–4 hours. For a quieter experience, the approach via the Lairig Ghru pass from the south offers a longer and more remote feel. Always check the Mountain Weather Information Service forecast before setting out, as the plateau can be dangerously icy in winter and surprisingly cold even in midsummer.

description: Despite its name meaning "little ridge", Aonach Beag is the seventh highest mountain in the British Isles at 1,234 meters. It sits in the shadow of its higher neighbor Aonach Mòr.

name: Aonach Mòr
description: Aonach Mòr is Scotland's eighth highest mountain. A ski resort operates on its slopes, and the Nevis Range gondola provides access to the mountain.

name: Carn Mòr Dearg
description: Famous for its knife-edge arête ridge, Carn Mòr Dearg is often climbed en route to Ben Nevis via the CMD Arête, one of Scotland's finest ridge walks. The ridge to Ben Nevis, the CMD Arete, is a narrow granite crest with the great North Face of Ben Nevis opposite.
history: Carn Mor Dearg stands directly opposite the great North Face of Ben Nevis, and the arete that links the two is one of the most celebrated high-level ridge walks in Scotland. The Charles Inglis Clark Memorial Hut, known as the CIC Hut, sits in the corrie below and serves climbers on the North Face.

The CMD Arete links Carn Mor Dearg with Ben Nevis

The CIC Hut serves climbers on the North Face
The name is usually translated as big red cairn
walking_guide:
The best-known route starts at the North Face car park near Torlundy, follows the Allt a' Mhuilinn path to the CIC Hut, and climbs to Carn Mor Dearg before following the CMD Arete to Ben Nevis. The descent is by the Ben Nevis Mountain Track, which needs transport arranged at the end. Allow eight to nine hours for the full circuit.

The arete is a Grade 1 scramble in good conditions, but it is exposed and needs a good head for heights. In winter it becomes a serious mountaineering route. Carn Mor Dearg is a good alternative for walkers who want a quieter day than the main Ben Nevis path.

name: Ben Lawers
description: Ben Lawers is the tenth highest mountain in Britain and the highest in the southern Highlands. It's famous for its arctic-alpine flora and was once thought to be Scotland's highest peak. It is the high point of a group of Munros above Loch Tay, and its lime-rich schist supports rare mountain plants found nowhere else in Britain.
history: Ben Lawers has long been valued by botanists for the rare arctic-alpine plants that grow on its crags, and the National Trust for Scotland looks after much of the mountain as a national nature reserve.
fun_facts: Ben Lawers is the highest mountain in the southern Highlands
The mountain is part of a National Nature Reserve managed by the National Trust for Scotland
Its schist rock supports rare alpine flowers
The summit is the tenth highest in Britain
The Ben Lawers range includes seven Munros, among them Beinn Ghlas and An Stuc
walking_guide:
Most walkers start at the National Trust for Scotland car park on the Ben Lawers road, high above Loch Tay, which saves around 400 metres of ascent. The path climbs over Beinn Ghlas to the main summit, with a return by the same route or by the Lawers Burn. Allow four to five hours for the round trip. The ground is well-defined, but the upper slopes are exposed and can be dangerous in winter.

Ben Lawers rewards a slow pace in early summer, when the rare alpine flowers on the crags are at their best and the limestone-rich slopes are green and bright. The route is one of the most accessible Munro days in Scotland, which makes it a popular first Munro, but it still has plenty of height and wind, so allow for that. Combining Beinn Ghlas and Ben Lawers is easy, and adding An Stuc makes a longer, more rugged day for confident walkers.

name: Beinn a' Bhuird
description: Beinn a' Bhuird has a massive plateau summit with huge granite cliffs on its northern face. It's one of the remotest Munros, requiring a long approach.

name: Lochnagar
description: Lochnagar is famous for its dramatic corrie and the dark lochan beneath its summit. The mountain has strong royal connections and inspired Lord Byron's poetry. It is one of the best-known summits of the Cairngorms National Park, and its granite cliffs, deep corrie and dark loch have shaped a serious winter climbing venue.
history: Lochnagar is a mountain with strong royal links. Queen Victoria walked in the area from Balmoral, and Prince Charles wrote a children's story, The Old Man of Lochnagar. Lord Byron, who spent part of his childhood in Aberdeenshire, wrote a famous poem about the mountain.
fun_facts: Lochnagar lies within the Cairngorms National Park near Balmoral
Prince Charles wrote the children's book The Old Man of Lochnagar
Lord Byron's poem about the hill brought it to wider attention
The northern corrie has granite cliffs popular with climbers
The summit cairn is named Cac Carn Beag
walking_guide:
The easiest ascent starts at the Spittal of Glenmuick car park and follows the Glas Allt path to a shoulder above the loch, before an easy ridge walk to the summit. Allow five to six hours for the round trip. A more dramatic route follows the cliff edge above the loch, with spectacular views into the corrie. The plateau is high and exposed, and snow can linger late in the season.

Lochnagar is a good choice for a first Cairngorms-area Munro, thanks to its straightforward start from Glen Muick, but the summit plateau is high, cold and often snowy well into spring. The path over the Meikle Pap is the standard and most direct route, and it is the one most walkers use. Keep away from the edge of the corrie, where snow can overhang the cliffs.

name: Bidean nam Bian
description: Bidean nam Bian is the highest peak in Argyll and the Glen Coe area. The mountain is hidden from the road by its three ridges, the Three Sisters of Glen Coe. Its three great buttresses face the A82 as the Three Sisters of Glen Coe, but the summit itself lies behind them, at the head of two corries.
history: Bidean nam Bian is the highest mountain in Argyll. It rises above the Glen Coe valley, where the 1692 Massacre of Glencoe took place, and Coire Gabhail, the Lost Valley, hidden between two of the Three Sisters, is said to have been used by the MacDonalds to hide cattle.
fun_facts: Bidean nam Bian is the highest mountain in Argyll
The Three Sisters of Glen Coe are three spurs of this mountain
Coire Gabhail, the Lost Valley, is a hidden glen reached by a steep path from the road
It has several subsidiary summits, including Stob Coire nan Lochan and Stob Coire Sgreamhach
Glen Coe is cared for by the National Trust for Scotland
walking_guide:
A well-liked circuit starts at the lay-by at the foot of Coire nan Lochan, climbs the burn to a high lochan under Stob Coire nan Lochan, then crosses to Bidean nam Bian and returns the same way or by Stob Coire Sgreamhach. The corrie path is steep and rocky, and in winter the whole mountain becomes a serious climb with avalanche risk. Allow seven to nine hours.

Glen Coe weather is often wet, so plan a fallback such as the Lost Valley walk, which makes a rewarding half day without any summit. The mountain is a good choice for walkers who already have a few Munros behind them and want a proper circuit with some scrambling on the upper ridges. In winter, check the Scottish Avalanche Information Service forecast and consider the mountain only with the right kit and experience. The nearby village has pubs and cafes, which makes it easy to base a weekend in the glen.

name: Ben Alder
description: Ben Alder is one of Scotland's most remote Munros, situated in wild country between Loch Ericht and Loch Laggan. The mountain has historical connections to Bonnie Prince Charlie.

name: Ben Cruachan
description: Ben Cruachan dominates the Pass of Brander and Loch Awe. The mountain has a vast horseshoe ridge and is home to the Cruachan Power Station hidden inside the mountain.
history: Ben Cruachan is best known for the Cruachan Power Station, a hydroelectric station built inside the mountain and opened in 1965. A dam high on the hillside holds the upper reservoir, and the station can be visited, which makes this one of the most unusual mountain days in Britain.
fun_facts: Cruachan Power Station is built inside the mountain
A dam holds the upper reservoir high on the hillside
The mountain has two Munros, Ben Cruachan and Stob Diamh
It overlooks the Pass of Brander and Loch Awe
The Falls of Cruachan railway station sits at the foot
walking_guide:
The classic horseshoe starts at the Falls of Cruachan station, follows the path to the dam, and climbs the ridge to Ben Cruachan before continuing to Stob Diamh. Allow seven to nine hours for the round trip. The ridge is narrow in places and requires some easy scrambling.

The upper slopes are steep and rocky, and the summit can be in cloud even on fine days. This is a satisfying day for walkers who have done a few Munros and want a proper ridge. The power station visitor centre is worth a visit if you have time.

name: Stob Coire Easain
description: A fine Munro with excellent views, Stob Coire Easain is usually climbed with nearby Stob a' Choire Mheadhoin. The approach follows the West Highland Line railway.

name: Snowdon
description: Yr Wyddfa (Snowdon) is the highest mountain in Wales at 1,085 meters. Part of Snowdonia National Park, it can be reached by six different walking paths or the historic Snowdon Mountain Railway.
history: The Welsh name "Yr Wyddfa" means "the tumulus" or "the burial place". According to legend, the giant Rhita Gawr is buried at the summit. The mountain railway opened in 1896, making Snowdon one of the most accessible high peaks in Britain.
fun_facts: Highest mountain in Wales
Can be reached by mountain railway since 1896
Has six main walking paths to the summit
The summit visitor centre was redesigned and reopened in 2009
On a clear day, you can see Ireland, Scotland, England and the Isle of Man
facilities: Car parks at multiple starting points
walking_guide:
Six main paths lead to the summit of Yr Wyddfa. The Llanberis Path is the longest and gentlest, around nine miles for the round trip, and follows the railway line. The Pyg Track and Miners' Track both start at Pen-y-Pass and join below the final climb, while the Watkin Path begins almost at sea level and gains the most height. The Rhyd Ddu and Snowdon Ranger paths are quieter, approaching from the west. Allow six to seven hours for most routes.

In summer Snowdon is busy, so start early and use the Sherpa bus rather than relying on the Pen-y-Pass car park, which fills very early. The summit has a visitor building, Hafod Eryri, and the Snowdon Mountain Railway runs from Llanberis. In winter the mountain is a serious mountaineering objective, with ice, snow and very strong winds, and walkers should only go with the right equipment and experience.

name: Schiehallion
description: Schiehallion is one of Scotland's best-known mountains, famous for its near-perfect cone shape. It was used in 1774 for the first accurate measurement of Earth's mass.
history: Schiehallion's symmetrical shape made it ideal for a scientific experiment in 1774, when astronomer Nevil Maskelyne measured the deflection of a plumb line beside the mountain to estimate the density of the Earth. The surveyor Charles Hutton developed contour lines to analyse the data, a technique now used on every map.
fun_facts: Schiehallion was used in 1774 to estimate the mass of the Earth
Contour lines were developed during the survey of the mountain
The name is often translated as fairy hill of the Caledonians
The east ridge is a rough boulder field
The path from Braes of Foss was rebuilt by the John Muir Trust
walking_guide:
The standard route starts at the Braes of Foss car park, following a well-built path up the east ridge to the summit. Allow four to five hours for the round trip. The upper section is a field of angular quartzite boulders, and it needs some care, especially when wet.

Schiehallion is a good first Munro, but the summit is exposed and the cloud can come down quickly. Take a map and compass, and wear boots with good grip. The mountain stands alone, so the views in all directions are superb on a clear day.

name: Carnedd Llewelyn
description: Carnedd Llewelyn is the second highest mountain in Wales. The vast summit area is part of the wild Carneddau range, popular with wild campers.

name: An Teallach
description: An Teallach is considered one of Scotland's finest mountains, with a spectacular ridge featuring dramatic pinnacles. The traverse requires scrambling and a good head for heights.
history: An Teallach, whose name means the forge, is regarded by many walkers as the finest mountain in the north-west Highlands. The ridge includes the Corrag Bhuidhe pinnacles, and Lord Berkeley's Seat, a sandstone ledge above the corrie, is a well-known viewpoint.
fun_facts: An Teallach means the forge
The main summits are Bidein a' Ghlas Thuill and Sgurr Fiona
The Corrag Bhuidhe pinnacles are a famous scramble
Lord Berkeley's Seat overlooks the corrie
The mountain stands above Dundonnell in Wester Ross
walking_guide:
The traverse starts at the Dundonnell car park and climbs to the ridge, passing both Munros before crossing the Corrag Bhuidhe pinnacles. A bypass path avoids the hardest scrambling. Allow eight to ten hours for the full ridge.

This is a serious mountain day with exposed scrambling, and it is best undertaken in good weather by experienced walkers. In winter it becomes a major mountaineering route, and the pinnacles can be dangerous in ice or snow.

name: Liathach
description: Liathach is one of the great Torridon mountains, with a terraced appearance and narrow ridge. The traverse is one of the finest mountain days in Scotland.
history: Liathach is one of the three great mountains of Torridon, with Beinn Eighe and Beinn Alligin. The mountain is formed of Torridonian sandstone capped with white quartzite, and the Torridon estate is cared for by the National Trust for Scotland.
fun_facts: Liathach is one of the great Torridon mountains
It has two Munros, Spidean a' Choire Leith and Mullach an Rathain
The Am Fasarinen pinnacles are the crux of the traverse
The mountain is formed of Torridonian sandstone and quartzite
The Torridon estate is cared for by the National Trust for Scotland
walking_guide:
The traverse of Liathach is one of the great ridge walks of Scotland, starting from the Glen Torridon car park and following a steep path to the main ridge. The Am Fasarinen pinnacles are a scramble that needs a good head for heights, although a bypass path avoids the worst of them. Allow seven to nine hours for the full traverse.

The ridge is narrow and exposed, and the weather in Torridon can be wild. This is a mountain for experienced walkers who are comfortable with scrambling, and it should be avoided in strong winds, mist, ice or snow unless you have the right skills.

name: Carnedd Dafydd
description: Carnedd Dafydd is part of the main Carneddau ridge. The mountain is often climbed with Carnedd Llewelyn, forming a fine ridge walk. It sits on the high ridge of the Carneddau, the largest area of land above 900 metres in Wales and England, and is home to the wild Carneddau ponies.
history: Carnedd Dafydd is traditionally said to be named after Dafydd ap Gruffudd, the brother of Llywelyn, the last prince of independent Wales, and it sits beside Carnedd Llewelyn, whose name is traditionally linked to Llywelyn himself. The ridge lies in the Carneddau, Snowdonia's largest and wildest upland area.
fun_facts: Carnedd Dafydd is the third highest mountain in Wales
It is named after a Welsh prince
Wild Carneddau ponies graze the high ground
Pen yr Ole Wen is the steep ascent from the Ogwen Valley
The ridge continues to Carnedd Llewelyn
walking_guide:
The classic route climbs Pen yr Ole Wen from Ogwen Cottage, then follows the ridge to Carnedd Dafydd and onward to Carnedd Llewelyn. Allow five to seven hours for the walk. The first ascent is steep and relentless, but the ridge beyond is broad and fairly gentle. The summit plateau is open and exposed to wind, and navigation can be tricky in mist.

Carnedd Dafydd is a very good choice for a day when the weather is settled, since the high ridge of the Carneddau is open and has few places to shelter. It is often quieter than the Glyderau or Snowdon, so it suits walkers who like space and long views. Walkers can extend the day by continuing to Carnedd Llewelyn and Yr Elen, or shorten it by returning by the Ffynnon Lloer route. Keep a respectful distance from the wild ponies.

name: Sgorr Dhearg
description: Part of the Beinn a' Bheithir ridge, Sgorr Dhearg offers stunning views over Loch Leven and Glen Coe. The ridge walk is airy and enjoyable.

name: Buachaille Etive Mòr
description: The "Great Herdsman of Etive" is one of Scotland's most iconic mountains, guarding the entrance to Glen Coe. Its pyramid shape is recognized worldwide.
history: The Buachaille Etive Mor, whose Gaelic name means the great herdsman of Etive, stands at the head of Glen Coe beside the A82. Its main summit, Stob Dearg, is one of the best-known peaks in Scotland and has long been a classic climbing venue.
fun_facts: Buachaille Etive Mor means great herdsman of Etive
The main summit is Stob Dearg
Curved Ridge is a classic scramble
Coire na Tulaich is the usual walking route
The mountain overlooks the start of Glen Coe
walking_guide:
The usual walkers' route climbs Coire na Tulaich from the road at Lagangarbh, near Altnafeadh. The path is steep and loose, and it becomes a serious winter gully when snow lies. Curved Ridge is a popular scramble on the right-hand side of the face. Allow five to six hours for the round trip.

The summit ridge is narrow and exposed, and the mountain is a significant undertaking for walkers who are new to Scottish Munros. Check the avalanche forecast in winter, and carry a map, compass and a head torch.

name: Beinn Eighe
description: Beinn Eighe was Britain's first National Nature Reserve. The mountain has white quartzite screes and a long multi-topped ridge requiring careful navigation.

name: Glyder Fawr
description: Glyder Fawr is the highest of the Glyderau range. The summit area has bizarre rock formations, including Cantilever Stone, one of Wales' most photographed features.
history: Glyder Fawr is the highest of the Glyderau and overlooks Cwm Idwal, a glacial hollow that has been studied by geologists for generations. The summit is a field of shattered rock, a product of frost action over thousands of years.
fun_facts: Glyder Fawr is the highest of the Glyderau
Cwm Idwal is one of the best examples of a glacial landscape in Britain
The Devil's Kitchen is a deep gully on the cliffs above Llyn Idwal
The summit is a field of frost-shattered rock
Glyder Fach is the neighbouring summit
walking_guide:
The usual route starts at Ogwen Cottage, passes Llyn Idwal and climbs beside the Devil's Kitchen, or follows the steep ridge of Y Gribin, to reach the high plateau. The summit is a jumble of rock slabs and boulders, and the round trip takes five to six hours.

Navigation on the plateau is difficult in mist, since paths are faint and the rocks hide the way. The cliffs of the Devil's Kitchen are steep and the rock is loose, so keep away from the edge. This is a fine day for walkers who want rugged scenery without a major scramble.

name: Glyder Fach
description: Glyder Fach has a rocky summit with the famous Cantilever Stone. The summit castle of rocks provides shelter and excellent scrambling opportunities.

name: Sgurr Dearg
description: Sgurr Dearg is famous for the Inaccessible Pinnacle on its summit, a vertical rock tower requiring rock climbing skills. It's the only Munro that must be climbed rather than walked.

name: Scafell Pike
description: Scafell Pike is the highest mountain in England at 978 meters. Located in the Lake District National Park, it forms part of the famous Three Peaks Challenge along with Ben Nevis and Snowdon.
history: The mountain takes its name from the Old Norse "Skalfjall" meaning "bald mountain". The summit was gifted to the National Trust in 1919 as a memorial to the men of the Lake District who died in World War I.
fun_facts: Highest peak in England
Part of the National Three Peaks Challenge
The first recorded ascent was by Samuel Taylor Coleridge in 1802
Named after the Old Norse for "bald mountain"
Over 250,000 people climb it each year
walking_guide:
The shortest route to the summit starts at Wasdale Head and climbs by Brown Tongue and Lingmell Col, taking around five to six hours for the round trip. A longer and more varied route starts at Seathwaite in Borrowdale and climbs via Esk Hause. Walkers from Langdale can also reach the top by the Esk Hause route, though the day is long. The upper section is a boulder field that can be slow going.

The summit and the surrounding land were given to the National Trust as a memorial to those who died in the First World War, and a plaque on the summit records this. The top is often in cloud, and navigation across the stony plateau needs care, so carry a map and compass and be ready to turn back. This is also one of the National Three Peaks, so expect crowds on summer weekends.

name: Ben Lomond
description: Ben Lomond is one of Scotland's most popular Munros, offering stunning views over Loch Lomond and the Trossachs. Its accessibility from Glasgow makes it a favorite for day hikes.
history: The name comes from the Gaelic "Beinn Laomainn" meaning "beacon mountain". It has been a popular climbing destination since the 18th century and was one of the first Munros many climbers ascend.
fun_facts: One of the most southerly Munros
Most popular Munro in Scotland by number of ascents
Owned and managed by the National Trust for Scotland
Takes about 6-7 hours for the round trip
Forms part of the Loch Lomond and The Trossachs National Park
walking_guide:
The usual route, known as the Tourist Route, starts at the Rowardennan car park on the east side of Loch Lomond and climbs steadily to the summit. It is a clear, well-made path and takes around five to six hours for the round trip. A quieter alternative is the Ptarmigan Ridge, which climbs the lower ridge before joining the main path.

Ben Lomond is the most southerly Munro and is easy to reach from Glasgow, so it is busy at weekends. The summit can be cold and windy, and cloud can come down quickly, so carry warm layers and a map and compass. The mountain is a good first Munro for walkers with some hillwalking experience.

name: Sgurr nan Gillean
description: Sgurr nan Gillean is one of the Black Cuillin peaks on Skye. The mountain requires scrambling and rock climbing skills, offering spectacular views over the island. The rock here is rough gabbro, which grips boots and hands far better than most mountain stone, but the narrow summit and the route finding on the approach make it a mountaineering objective rather than a walk.
history: Sgurr nan Gillean is the northernmost peak of the Black Cuillin on the Isle of Skye and the first of the Cuillin summits to be climbed in recorded history, by Professor James David Forbes in 1836. The name is usually translated from Gaelic as peak of the young men. Its pinnacled outline is the most photographed view from the Sligachan Hotel and the old bridge beside it.
fun_facts: Sgurr nan Gillean is the northernmost of the Black Cuillin Munros on Skye
The first recorded ascent was by Professor J. D. Forbes in 1836
The Cuillin are formed of gabbro, a rock with a notably rough, grippy surface
The normal route, the West Ridge, is usually graded as a Grade 3 scramble
Pinnacle Ridge on the eastern side is a more serious route used by experienced scramblers
walking_guide:
The usual route begins at Sligachan, follows the path from the hotel towards the mountain's western flank, and climbs the West Ridge, a sustained scramble with some exposed moves near the top. Allow around seven to nine hours for the round trip from Sligachan. The final section has steep ground on both sides, and a rope is often used by less confident parties. Navigation is difficult in mist because the ridge is rocky and compass readings can be unreliable on magnetic gabbro. This is a day for good weather and a competent party.

This is not a mountain for a first Scottish scramble. Walkers who have done Aonach Eagach, Crib Goch or Sharp Edge in comfort will find the West Ridge a step up, with longer and more consequential exposure, and many people hire a mountain guide for it. Check the forecast carefully, since wet gabbro is still grippy but wind on the pinnacles is dangerous. Midges are bad around Sligachan in still summer weather, so late spring and early autumn are more pleasant.

name: Helvellyn
description: Helvellyn is the third highest peak in England and one of the most popular mountains in the Lake District. The mountain offers several challenging routes including the famous Striding Edge. Two knife-edge arms, Striding Edge and Swirral Edge, wrap around the eastern corrie and hold Red Tarn, which is why the peak has such a pull for walkers who want a proper mountain day without technical climbing.
history: The mountain has been a popular destination since the 18th century. In 1926, an aircraft landed on the summit plateau, and a memorial stone commemorates this event. The name possibly derives from the Celtic "hal" meaning moorland.
fun_facts: Third highest mountain in England
Features the famous Striding Edge ridge walk
An airplane landed on the summit in 1926
Can be climbed year-round but requires winter skills in cold months
Over 250,000 walkers climb it annually
facilities: Car parks at Glenridding and Patterdale
walking_guide:
The classic round starts at Glenridding or Patterdale, climbs to Hole-in-the-Wall and follows Striding Edge to the summit, then drops by Swirral Edge to Red Tarn and returns beside Glenridding Beck. Allow five to six hours. The edge itself is a hands-on scramble above steep drops: choose a dry, calm day, and know that a lower path skirts the crest if the wind picks up. A gentler alternative is the western approach from Wythburn, which avoids the exposure but climbs steadily for most of its length. The summit plateau is wide and flat, and in cloud it is easy to wander towards the edges, so navigate carefully.

Choosing between the routes comes down to confidence on exposed ground. Striding Edge suits walkers who are happy using their hands and keeping calm with drops on both sides, while Swirral Edge is shorter and best used for the descent. Winter conditions turn both edges into serious mountaineering ground that needs an ice axe, crampons and the skills to use them, so most visitors do better to wait for summer or take the Wythburn path instead. Start early on fine weekends, because the Glenridding car parks fill quickly.

name: Sgurr Mhic Choinnich
description: One of the Black Cuillin peaks, Sgurr Mhic Choinnich is a rocky summit requiring scrambling. The peak is often climbed as part of the Cuillin Ridge traverse.

name: Y Garn
description: Y Garn overlooks Llyn Ogwen and has a distinctive pyramidal shape. The Devil's Kitchen cleft on the northeast face is a famous climbing venue.

name: Ill Crag
description: Ill Crag is part of the Scafell massif and one of England's highest summits. It's usually climbed as part of a round from Wasdale or Borrowdale. It lies between Broad Crag and Esk Hause on the high ground of the Scafell massif.
history: Ill Crag is one of the high tops of the Scafell massif, between Scafell Pike and Esk Hause. It is a subsidiary summit of Scafell Pike and is often passed over by walkers heading for England's highest mountain, but it is an excellent viewpoint in its own right.
fun_facts: Ill Crag is one of the highest summits in England
It lies on the ridge between Scafell Pike and Esk Hause
Broad Crag is its neighbour
The summit has views into Eskdale and Wasdale
It is often climbed as part of a round of the Scafell massif
walking_guide:
Ill Crag is normally climbed as part of a longer day on Scafell Pike, from Seathwaite in Borrowdale or Wasdale Head. The route follows the ridge from Esk Hause over Ill Crag and Broad Crag to Scafell Pike. Allow six to eight hours for the full round.

The ground is rocky and the paths are rough, so wear sturdy boots and carry a map and compass. The summit area is frequently cloudy, and the boulder fields can be difficult to navigate in poor visibility.

name: Skiddaw
description: Skiddaw is one of the Lake District's most prominent mountains and one of the easiest to climb. The mountain overlooks Keswick and Derwentwater. It rises above Keswick, a broad dome of Skiddaw slate whose smooth, rounded slopes contrast with the craggier fells further south.
history: Skiddaw is built from Skiddaw slate, among the oldest rocks in the Lake District, which weathers into the smooth, scree-covered slopes that give the mountain its distinctive profile. It has been a popular ascent for visitors since the early days of Lakeland tourism and is climbed in large numbers because of its straightforward paths from the edge of Keswick.
fun_facts: Skiddaw is one of the highest mountains in England
It is made of Skiddaw slate, some of the oldest rocks in the Lake District
The mountain is climbed from Keswick on a wide, well-made path
Its bulk dominates the view north of Derwentwater and Keswick
Skiddaw is part of the Northern Fells, a group of rounded hills far gentler than the central Lakeland peaks
walking_guide:
The usual route up Skiddaw starts from the car park at the end of Gale Road, above Keswick, and follows a broad track past Latrigg before climbing steadily to the summit ridge. The path is wide and clear, and the gradient is moderate throughout, which makes this one of the easier ways onto a major Lakeland summit. Allow roughly four to five hours for the round trip. The top of Skiddaw is exposed to wind and cloud, so carry waterproofs and warm layers even on a bright day, and take a map and compass in case of poor visibility.

Skiddaw is the best choice in the Lake District for walkers who want a big summit without any scrambling. The path is straightforward in summer, but the mountain is exposed and can be very windy and cold, and many people underestimate the walk. Start early to avoid the heat and the crowds on summer weekends. The mountain is also popular with fell runners, so be prepared to share the path.

name: Beinn Liath Mhòr
description: A sprawling Corbett in the Fannichs with a long summit ridge. The mountain offers good views of the surrounding peaks and is usually climbed from Glen Fannich.

name: Elidir Fawr
description: Elidir Fawr is the northernmost of the major Snowdonia peaks. Inside the mountain is the Dinorwig Power Station, a massive pumped-storage facility.

name: Crib Goch
description: Crib Goch is the most famous knife-edge ridge in Wales. The exposed scramble is the classic route up Snowdon but requires a good head for heights. The ridge forms the northern arm of the Snowdon Horseshoe and is regarded as one of the most exposed scrambles in Britain.
history: Crib Goch, whose name means red ridge in Welsh, is the first part of the Snowdon Horseshoe. The hotel at Pen-y-Gwryd, close to the foot of the ridge, was used as a training base by the 1953 Everest expedition, a link that adds to the area's mountaineering heritage.
fun_facts: Crib Goch means red ridge in Welsh
It is the first section of the Snowdon Horseshoe
The scramble is exposed and graded as a serious undertaking
The Pen-y-Gwryd Hotel was used by the 1953 Everest team for training
In winter conditions the ridge becomes a serious mountaineering route
walking_guide:
Crib Goch is usually climbed from Pen-y-Pass by the Pyg Track and a rising path onto the ridge. The knife-edge scrambling requires a good head for heights and should only be attempted in dry, calm weather. Allow time for the traverse to Garnedd Ugain and Snowdon, and consider the Pyg Track as a safer alternative if conditions or confidence are poor.

Crib Goch is a scramble, not a walk, and the crossing is dangerous in wind, rain, snow or ice. Walkers who have never scrambled before should start on easier ridges, or hire a guide. Once on the ridge, there is no easy escape, so you should be committed before you set off. The Snowdon Horseshoe is best done on a clear, dry, calm day, ideally in summer.

name: Tryfan
description: Tryfan is one of Wales' most famous mountains, requiring scrambling to reach the summit. Adam and Eve, two monoliths on the summit, are traditionally jumped between. Few mountains in Britain have such a clear scrambling line, and the rocky summit is crowned with two standing stones known as Adam and Eve.
history: Tryfan rises directly from the A5 in the Ogwen Valley and has long been a training ground for climbers. The two upright stones on its summit are called Adam and Eve, and a long-standing tradition is to jump from one to the other, an act that carries real risk.
fun_facts: Tryfan rises straight from the Ogwen Valley in a single steep line
The summit is topped by two standing stones, Adam and Eve
The North Ridge is a classic Grade 1 scramble
Tryfan is one of the few Welsh mountains with no easy walking route to the top
The Heather Terrace offers a rough path on the western side
walking_guide:
The North Ridge is the classic route, climbing from the A5 near Llyn Ogwen over a series of rocky steps to the summit. It is a hands-on scramble and not a walk, and most people take three to four hours for the ascent. The descent is usually by the south ridge to Bwlch Tryfan, or by the Heather Terrace path.

Tryfan is a popular mountain with walkers, but it needs a head for heights and care in wet weather, when the rock is slippery. It is not advisable to attempt it in mist, snow or ice unless you have scrambling experience. Many walkers combine Tryfan with the Glyderau, but this makes a long day.

name: Beinn Dearg (Torridon)
description: A magnificent Corbett in Torridon with superb views of the main Torridon peaks. The mountain offers a rewarding day out with less crowds than the nearby Munros. The views across Glen Torridon to the great Torridon mountains are the main attraction of the day.
history: Beinn Dearg is a Corbett in the Torridon area, in a landscape dominated by the giants of Liathach, Beinn Eighe and Beinn Alligin. The surrounding rock is Torridonian sandstone, among the oldest rock in Britain, and the hills here have a stark, weathered quality.
fun_facts: Beinn Dearg is a Corbett in the Torridon area
The surrounding hills are made of ancient Torridonian sandstone
Liathach, Beinn Eighe and Beinn Alligin are the neighbouring giants
It is far quieter than the nearby Munros
The views of the Torridon peaks make it popular with photographers
walking_guide:
Beinn Dearg is a good choice for walkers who want views of the great Torridon peaks without the crowds. Check a current guidebook or Walkhighlands for the best approach, as paths vary and some sections are rough. Allow around five to six hours for the round trip.

The weather in Torridon is changeable and the rock can be slippery when wet. Carry a map and compass, and be prepared for navigation in mist on the upper slopes.

name: Foinaven
description: Foinaven is a remote and spectacular mountain in Sutherland, featuring white quartzite screes and dramatic corries. The mountain requires a long approach through wild country. Its pale quartzite screes shine in sunlight and give the long ridge a look quite unlike the darker mountains of the north-west Highlands.
history: Foinaven lies in the Reay Forest, a vast area of deer forest and moorland in the far north-west. It is one of the finest Corbetts in Scotland and is considered by many walkers to be among the best mountain days in the Highlands. Its remote setting and long approach keep visitor numbers low.
fun_facts: Foinaven is a Corbett in the Reay Forest of Sutherland
Its quartzite screes are very pale compared with most Highland mountains
The main top, Ganu Mor, is the high point of the ridge
The long approach makes it one of the more remote Corbetts
The area is part of the North West Highlands Geopark
walking_guide:
The usual route starts at the Gualin lay-by on the A838, follows the stalkers' path towards Strath Dionard, then climbs the ridge to Ganu Mor. Allow six to eight hours for a long day in remote country with no phone signal. The scree can be loose and tiring, and the weather changes quickly. Carry spare layers and tell someone your plan before you leave.

Foinaven is a long, committing day in a remote area, so it suits experienced hill walkers who are happy navigating without a clear path in places. The ground is wild and rough, and a day in the Reay Forest can mean seeing no other walkers at all. Check stalking information before you go, because access may be restricted during the deer season, and expect a long drive from Inverness or Ullapool. The reward is a ridge of unusual white rock and a sense of space that is rare in the UK.

name: Great End
description: Great End is at the head of Borrowdale with impressive crags. Often climbed with Scafell Pike, it gives spectacular views down the valley.
history: Great End is the northernmost summit of the Scafell range and has a steep, craggy north face that attracts climbers in winter. Seathwaite, the usual starting point, is known as one of the wettest inhabited places in England.
fun_facts: Great End has a steep craggy north face
Sprinkling Tarn lies beneath the summit
Seathwaite is among the wettest inhabited places in England
Esk Hause is the pass beside the mountain
Great End's gullies are a popular winter climbing venue
walking_guide:
Great End is usually climbed from Seathwaite in Borrowdale by the path to Sty Head and Sprinkling Tarn, then up to the summit. Allow five to six hours. Many walkers combine it with Scafell Pike, which makes a long day.

The crags on the north face are steep, and in winter the gullies hold snow and ice. Keep away from the edge in mist, and navigate carefully on the stony ground.

name: Aran Fawddwy
description: Aran Fawddwy is the highest peak in the Aran range and southern Snowdonia. The mountain is more remote and less visited than the northern peaks. It stands at the head of the Cwm Cywarch valley, with steep north-east crags that fall to Creiglyn Dyfi, the small lake that is the source of the River Dyfi.
history: Aran Fawddwy lies in the southern Snowdonia uplands, far from the busy northern paths. The Afon Dyfi rises on its flank, at Creiglyn Dyfi, and the mountain forms a twin pair with neighbouring Aran Benllyn, the Arans ridge.
fun_facts: Aran Fawddwy is the highest peak in the Aran range
The River Dyfi rises at Creiglyn Dyfi beneath the summit
Aran Benllyn is its neighbouring peak on the same ridge
It is the highest mountain in Wales south of the Snowdon massif
The Cwm Cywarch route is the classic approach
walking_guide:
The classic walk starts in Cwm Cywarch, climbs onto the ridge, then follows the crest to the summit, with a return by the same route or by a loop via Drysgol. Allow four to five hours. The ridge is steep in places but straightforward in clear weather, and the views to the Dyfi valley are among the best in mid Wales.

Aran Fawddwy is a quiet and rewarding alternative to Snowdon for walkers who want a big Welsh summit without the crowds. The Cwm Cywarch approach is the most scenic, with the crags and waterfalls of the valley head giving way to long open ridges. Combining Aran Fawddwy with Aran Benllyn makes a classic ridge walk, but it needs transport at both ends or a long return along the road. The area has limited phone signal, so tell someone your plan before setting out.

name: Bowfell
description: Bowfell is a beautiful mountain at the head of Langdale. The summit is a rocky pyramid with excellent views, and the route via The Band is classic.
history: Bowfell stands at the head of Great Langdale and is one of the best-known mountains in the central Lake District. Its summit is a rocky cone, and the Great Slab and Bowfell Buttress on its northern flank are well known to climbers.
fun_facts: Bowfell is a rocky pyramid at the head of Great Langdale
The Band is the classic walkers' route
Bowfell Buttress is a well-known climbing crag
Three Tarns lies between Bowfell and Crinkle Crags
The summit has views to Scafell Pike and the western fells
walking_guide:
The usual route starts at the Old Dungeon Ghyll car park, climbs the ridge known as The Band, and reaches the summit after a steady ascent. Allow five to six hours for the round trip. The path is clear but steep, and the final section is a boulder field.

The summit is exposed to the wind, and the weather can change quickly. Combine Bowfell with the Crinkle Crags for a longer and more rewarding day. Walkers should avoid the crags in mist and keep to the path.

name: Great Gable
description: Great Gable is one of the Lake District's most iconic mountains. Its distinctive shape dominates the head of Wasdale, and it was gifted to the National Trust as a war memorial.
history: The summit of Great Gable carries a memorial to members of the Fell and Rock Climbing Club who died in the First World War. The club also gave the surrounding fells to the National Trust, and a Remembrance Sunday service is held at the memorial each year, attended by walkers who make the climb in all weather.
fun_facts: Great Gable has a war memorial on its summit
A Remembrance Sunday service is held there each year
Napes Needle on the southern face is a famous rock climb
The mountain is one of the best viewpoints in the Lake District
Sty Head is the pass at its foot
walking_guide:
The shortest route starts at Seathwaite in Borrowdale and climbs via Sty Head to the summit by the steep path on the south side. From Wasdale Head the Gavel Neese path is steep and direct. A longer alternative starts at Honister Pass and traverses Grey Knotts and Windy Gap. Allow five to six hours for the round trip.

The upper slopes are steep and stony, and the summit is often in cloud. Navigation can be difficult in mist, and the crags on the Wasdale side are dangerous for anyone who strays off the path. This is a good mountain for confident walkers who want a classic Lakeland summit.

name: Cadair Idris
description: Cadair Idris is 893 metres (2,930 feet) high — one of the most iconic mountains in Wales and the second most climbed peak in Snowdonia National Park after Snowdon. Also known as Cader Idris, it sits at the southern end of the Snowdonia range in Gwynedd, overlooking the Mawddach Estuary and the market town of Dolgellau. Its summit, Pen y Gadair, offers sweeping views across Cardigan Bay to the Llŷn Peninsula on a clear day. The name Cadair Idris translates from Welsh as "the chair of Idris," referring to a legendary giant said to have used the summit as his throne.
history: The name means "Chair of Idris" in Welsh, referring to a giant from Welsh mythology. The mountain has been a tourist destination since Victorian times and inspired many poets and artists including Richard Wilson and J.M.W. Turner. The mountain's true summit, Pen y Gadair, sits at the head of a dramatic horseshoe of cliffs enclosing Llyn Cau, a glacial lake formed during the last ice age. Snowdonia National Park adopted the "Cader Idris" spelling on its official signage in 2016, reflecting the local Meirionnydd dialect pronunciation, though "Cadair Idris" remains the standard Welsh orthographic form.

Legend says anyone who spends a night alone on the mountain wakes either a poet or a madman — or does not wake at all

Has three main walking routes: the Pony Path, the Minffordd Path, and the Fox's Path from Dol Idris
Popular with Victorian tourists and artists, including J.M.W. Turner who painted the mountain in 1798
Home to rare arctic-alpine plants including the Snowdon lily and purple saxifrage

Cadair Idris is part of the Welsh Three Peaks Challenge alongside Snowdon and Pen y Fan
famous_for: the legend that sleeping on its summit makes you a poet or a madman
walking_guide:
The Pony Path from Ty Nant is the most popular and easiest route up Cadair Idris, one of the finest mountains in Snowdonia National Park. It starts from the Ty Nant car park (LL40 1TN) near Dolgellau and follows a well-graded path northwards through bracken and oak woodland before emerging onto open hillside. The trail climbs steadily to a broad ridge, then turns west to reach Pen y Gadair, the 893m summit, in roughly 3–4 hours. The round trip is about 9km and takes 5–6 hours. Cadair Idris difficulty on the Pony Path is moderate — no scrambling is required, and the gradient is the gentlest of the three main routes.

The Minffordd Path from the south is shorter but steeper, climbing alongside Llyn Cau before a short scramble to the summit — arguably the most scenic route, with dramatic views of the glacial corrie and Llyn Cau far below. The Minffordd Path is the route most experienced walkers prefer for its drama and scenery, though the Cadair Idris difficulty is higher than the Pony Path due to steeper terrain and a short rocky section near the top.

Fox's Path is the steepest and most direct, with loose scree near the summit; it should be ascended rather than descended. All three routes reward you with panoramic views across Cardigan Bay to the Llŷn Peninsula, and on a clear day you can see the Preseli Hills in Pembrokeshire and the Wicklow Mountains in Ireland. Check the Met Office mountain forecast before setting out, as Cadair Idris catches weather from both the Irish Sea and the interior of Snowdonia.

faqs.question: How tall is Cadair Idris?
faqs.answer: Cadair Idris is 893 metres (2,930 feet) high at its summit, Pen y Gadair, according to Ordnance Survey data. This makes it one of the highest mountains in Wales, though it is 192m lower than Snowdon (1,085m).

faqs.question: What is the height of Cadair Idris in feet?
faqs.answer: The height of Cadair Idris is 2,930 feet (893 metres) above sea level. The Cader Idris height is the same regardless of which spelling you use — both refer to the same mountain.

faqs.question: Is it Cadair Idris or Cader Idris?
faqs.answer: Both are correct. Cadair is the standard Welsh spelling; Cader reflects the local Meirionnydd dialect and is also used on Snowdonia National Park signage, which adopted the Cader Idris spelling officially in 2016.

faqs.question: How tall is Mount Cader Idris?
faqs.answer: Mount Cader Idris reaches 893m (2,930 ft) at its highest summit, Pen y Gadair. It is the 19th-highest mountain in Wales but one of the two most popular after Snowdon.

faqs.question: How difficult is Cadair Idris to climb?
faqs.answer: Cadair Idris difficulty is rated moderate on the standard Pony Path — no scrambling is required and the gradient is gradual. The Minffordd Path is steeper with a short scramble near the summit, and Fox's Path is the most challenging with loose scree. A reasonable level of fitness is needed for all routes.

faqs.question: Is Cadair Idris part of the Welsh Three Peaks Challenge?
faqs.answer: Yes — it's commonly climbed as part of the Welsh Three Peaks Challenge alongside Snowdon (Yr Wyddfa, 1,085m) and Pen y Fan (886m) in the Brecon Beacons.

faqs.question: How long does it take to climb Cadair Idris?
faqs.answer: The Pony Path round trip takes 5–6 hours for fit walkers, covering roughly 9km with 720m of ascent. The Minffordd Path is similar in time but shorter in distance with steeper terrain.

faqs.question: Which is the easiest route up Cadair Idris?
faqs.answer: The Pony Path from Ty Nant is the easiest of the three main routes — it has no scrambling, a steadier gradient, and is the standard choice for most walkers. The Minffordd Path is more scenic but harder, and Fox's Path is the steepest and should generally be climbed, not descended, because of loose scree near the summit.

faqs.question: Where is Cadair Idris?
faqs.answer: Cadair Idris is in Gwynedd, Wales, at the southern end of Snowdonia National Park (Eryri). The nearest town is Dolgellau, and the parking postcode for the Pony Path trailhead at Ty Nant is LL40 1TN.

faqs.question: Is Cadair Idris higher than Snowdon?
faqs.answer: No. Snowdon (Yr Wyddfa) at 1,085m is 192m higher than Cadair Idris at 893m. However, many hillwalkers consider Cadair Idris a wilder and more rewarding climb due to its dramatic cliffs, quieter paths, and rich folklore.
