The ridge between Corn Du and Pen y Fan is a short, simple link
walking_guide:
Corn Du is usually climbed from the Pont ar Daf car park, following the main path up the steep final slope to the summit. It takes around two hours for the ascent, and many walkers continue to Pen y Fan across the short col. A return by Cwm Llwch gives a quieter loop with views of the lake.

The summit is exposed and the north face drops steeply, so keep away from the edge in mist. Corn Du is a good choice for walkers who want a shorter day than the full horseshoe, and it is a good place to watch the sunrise on a clear morning.

name: Moel Siabod
description: Moel Siabod is an isolated peak offering superb views of Snowdon. The mountain is easily accessible from Capel Curig and provides excellent walking.

name: Blencathra
description: Blencathra, also known as Saddleback, has several ridges offering varied routes. Sharp Edge provides one of the Lake District's finest scrambles. Its southern face rises steeply above the village of Threlkeld, split by a series of ridges and gullies, and the long, sweeping profile that gives the fell its alternative name of Saddleback.
history: Blencathra is also known as Saddleback because, from the east or west, its summit ridge dips like the seat of a saddle. The name Blencathra is thought to be of ancient Brittonic origin. Alfred Wainwright regarded it as one of his favourite fells, and it features prominently in his Pictorial Guide to the Lakeland Fells.
fun_facts: Blencathra is also called Saddleback because of the dip along its summit ridge
Sharp Edge, on the Scales Tarn side, is one of the best-known scrambles in the Lake District
Hall's Fell Ridge is a classic route to the summit that gains height steadily from Threlkeld
The fell is a Wainwright, a Hewitt, a Nuttall and a Marilyn
Blencathra is a Wainwright in the Northern Fells, a short drive from Keswick
walking_guide:
The most popular ascent of Blencathra starts at Threlkeld and climbs Hall's Fell Ridge, a long and continuous rising ridge that reaches the summit with only light scrambling in places. Many walkers prefer to return by the gentler path to the east or down via Gategill. Sharp Edge, approached from Scales Tarn near Mungrisdale, is a narrow arete that needs a good head for heights and is best avoided in wet, icy or windy weather. Allow around four to five hours for a round trip by Hall's Fell. Carry a map and compass, check the Met Office mountain forecast before you set off, and expect cold, exposed conditions on the summit ridge even on fine days.

Blencathra suits walkers who want a Lake District fell with real character rather than a gentle path. Hall's Fell Ridge is a good introduction to ridge walking, but it is steep and rocky, and the grassy summit ridge above can be windy. Sharp Edge has a reputation as one of the harder scrambles in the Lakes, and the main problem is the exposed final step; walkers who are unsure should take the Hall's Fell route instead. Threlkeld has good parking and a pub.

name: Crinkle Crags
description: Crinkle Crags is a mountain with five main "crinkles" or summits. The route involves scrambling and is one of Lakeland's finest ridge walks.
history: Crinkle Crags takes its name from the five crinkles, or rocky summits, on its ridge. The Bad Step, a short scramble on the ridge, is the crux of the route, and the mountain is generally regarded as one of the finest ridge walks in Lakeland.
fun_facts: Crinkle Crags has five main crinkles on its ridge
The Bad Step is a short scramble on the ridge
Three Tarns lies between Crinkle Crags and Bowfell
Great Langdale is the usual starting point
The ridge is often combined with Bowfell
walking_guide:
The usual route starts at the Old Dungeon Ghyll car park and climbs by Oxendale and the Great Knott to the ridge. The Bad Step is a short but awkward scramble, and walkers can avoid it by a bypass path. Allow six to seven hours for the round trip.

The ridge is rocky and the weather can be wild. Navigation in mist is hard since the crinkles look similar. This is a good day for confident walkers who want a ridge with a bit of scrambling.

name: Grasmoor
description: Grasmoor is the highest of the northwestern fells. The mountain has steep sides, particularly Dove Crags, and commands excellent views. It rises above Crummock Water and Buttermere, and its steep western face is one of the more dramatic sights in the north-western fells.
history: Grasmoor overlooks the Buttermere valley and Crummock Water in the north-western Lake District. The land beneath it includes Rannerdale, where a famous display of bluebells appears each spring,.
fun_facts: Grasmoor is the highest of the north-western fells
The steep Dove Crags drop away on its southern flank
Rannerdale, beneath the mountain, is known for its spring bluebells
Crummock Water lies directly beneath the western face
The summit looks out across the Buttermere valley to High Stile and Red Pike
walking_guide:
A common route starts at the Lanthwaite Green car park, crosses the beck, and climbs the Lad Hows ridge to the summit plateau, a steep but straightforward grassy slope. The return can be made by the same path or by a loop round Whiteless Pike. Allow around four hours for the main ascent and descent.

Grasmoor is one of the best Lake District fells for walkers who want long views without a crowd. The western face is steep, so take care on the descent in wet weather, and avoid the rocky ground near Dove Crags in cloud.

name: Cul Mor
description: Cul Mor is the highest of the Assynt Corbetts. The approach passes spectacular sandstone scenery, and the summit gives panoramic views. The sandstone landscape of Coigach and Assynt around it is among the most distinctive in Britain.
history: Cul Mor is the highest of the Corbetts in this part of Coigach and Assynt. Nearby Knockan Crag is a National Nature Reserve where visitors can see the Moine Thrust, a geological feature that helped to change scientists' understanding of how mountains are formed.
fun_facts: Cul Mor is a Corbett in Coigach and Assynt
Knockan Crag, nearby, is famous for the Moine Thrust
The mountain is built from Torridonian sandstone
Cul Beag is its smaller neighbour
The summit has far-reaching views over Assynt and Coigach
walking_guide:
Cul Mor is usually climbed from Knockan, with a path leading across the moor towards the foot of the mountain. The ascent is steady, and the final slopes are steep and rocky. Allow around six hours for the round trip.

The views from the top are among the best in the region, and the area around Knockan Crag is worth a stop on the drive. Check a current guidebook for the latest route details, since paths can be faint.

name: High Street
description: High Street follows a Roman road and has one of the Lake District's longest summit ridges. The mountain offers easy walking with extensive views.
history: High Street takes its name from a Roman road that crosses its ridge, linking the forts at Ambleside and Brougham. The broad summit was once used for horse races, and the nearby area is known as Racecourse Hill. Below the mountain, Haweswater reservoir drowned the village of Mardale Green in the 1930s.
fun_facts: A Roman road runs along the summit ridge
Racecourse Hill on the summit was once used for horse races
Haweswater reservoir drowned the village of Mardale Green
Riggindale was long the only place in England where golden eagles nested
The summit ridge is one of the longest in the Lake District
walking_guide:
The classic route starts at Mardale Head at the end of Haweswater and climbs the ridge of Long Stile, with views down to Riggindale. The summit is a broad plateau, and the return can be made by Mardale Ill Bell. Allow five to six hours for the round trip.

The ridge is exposed, and the weather can change quickly. This is a gentle mountain in terms of scrambling, so it suits walkers who want a long, high-level walk with history.

name: Quinag
description: Quinag is a complex mountain with three main tops. The Y-shaped ridge offers superb walking with dramatic views over the Assynt landscape.

name: Coniston Old Man
description: Coniston Old Man towers over the village of Coniston and its lake. Mining remains on its slopes tell of its industrial past, while the summit gives superb views.
history: The slopes of Coniston Old Man are scarred by slate quarries and copper mines, which were worked for centuries. The Coppermines valley beneath the mountain holds many of the remains. Coniston village and its lake are linked with John Ruskin, who lived at Brantwood, and with Donald Campbell, who died on Coniston Water in 1967.
fun_facts: Coniston Old Man was heavily mined for slate and copper
Low Water tarn lies in a hollow beneath the summit
John Ruskin lived at Brantwood on Coniston Water
Donald Campbell died on Coniston Water in 1967
The summit gives views to Morecambe Bay on clear days
walking_guide:
The usual route starts in Coniston village and follows the path up Church Beck and through the Coppermines valley to Low Water and the summit. Allow four to five hours for the round trip. The path is clear and well-made, though the old mine workings are dangerous and best avoided.

The summit is exposed to the wind, and the weather can be severe even in summer. This is a good choice for walkers who want a classic Lakeland day with a lot of history.

name: Cribyn
description: Cribyn has a sharp pointed summit and is often climbed with Pen y Fan. The mountain forms part of the classic Brecon Beacons horseshoe walk. Its steep, pointed summit gives it the look of a classic peak,.
fun_facts: Cribyn has a steep, pointed summit above the Bwlch ar y Fan col
The classic horseshoe route links Cribyn with Pen y Fan and Corn Du
The Neuadd Reservoirs lie beneath its eastern flank
Bwlch ar y Fan is the col between Cribyn and Pen y Fan
The ascent from the col is short but steep
walking_guide:
Cribyn can be climbed from the Neuadd Reservoirs car park, following the track to the col at Bwlch ar y Fan and then climbing the steep eastern slope. The ascent is short but steep, and the path is eroded in places. Many walkers include Cribyn in the full Beacons horseshoe, which takes five to six hours and links Cribyn, Pen y Fan and Corn Du.

The views from Cribyn are among the best in the Brecon Beacons, and the summit is often quieter than Pen y Fan. Descents from the summit are steep, so wear boots with good grip.

name: Cul Beag
description: Cul Beag is smaller than its neighbor Cul Mor but offers equally fine views. The mountain has dramatic cliffs on its northern side. Its steep northern crags give the hill a rugged character that belies its height, and the views over the lochans of Coigach are superb.
history: Cul Beag is a Corbett in Coigach, in the far north-west Highlands, and sits close to Stac Pollaidh and Cul Mor. The hills in this area are made of ancient Torridonian sandstone, and the landscape of isolated peaks rising from a moorland of lochans is one of the most distinctive in Scotland.
fun_facts: Cul Beag is a Corbett in Coigach, near Ullapool
Its northern face is a line of steep crags
Cul Mor is its larger neighbour
Stac Pollaidh lies just to the west
The surrounding landscape of lochans and sandstone peaks is among the most distinctive in the Highlands
walking_guide:
Cul Beag is usually climbed from the lay-by at Linneraineach on the A835, from where a path leads towards the foot of the hill. The final ascent is steep and rocky in places. Allow around four hours for the round trip.

The views from the summit are outstanding, with Suilven, Stac Pollaidh and the Summer Isles all in sight. Cul Beag is a good choice for walkers who want a shorter day in a remote setting.

name: Ben Loyal
description: Known as the "Queen of Scottish Mountains", Ben Loyal has four distinctive peaks. The mountain dominates the landscape of northwest Sutherland.

name: Ben More Coigach
description: Ben More Coigach is a remote mountain accessed via a long walk through the Coigach hills. The summit provides spectacular views over the Summer Isles. Its sharp, rocky ridge rises straight above the sea, and the view of the Summer Isles is the main reward.
history: Ben More Coigach is a Corbett that rises above the coast at Achiltibuie, with views across the Summer Isles. The mountain is part of the ancient Torridonian landscape of Coigach, a peninsula in the far north-west Highlands.
fun_facts: Ben More Coigach is a Corbett above Achiltibuie
The Summer Isles lie below the summit
The mountain is built from Torridonian sandstone
The ridge has a rocky, jagged skyline
Coigach is a peninsula in the far north-west Highlands
walking_guide:
Ben More Coigach is normally climbed from the road near Achiltibuie, with a path leading to the summit ridge. The ridge has some easy scrambling, and the final section is steep. Allow around five to six hours for the round trip.

The views to the Summer Isles are superb, but the summit ridge is exposed and the weather on the coast can change quickly. Take a map and compass, and avoid the ridge in strong winds.

name: Whernside
description: Whernside is the highest of the Yorkshire Three Peaks. The walk along the ridge from Ribblehead Viaduct is spectacular, with panoramic views. The long, whale-backed ridge is one of the Three Peaks and is best known for the view down to Ribblehead Viaduct.
history: Whernside is the highest of the Yorkshire Three Peaks. The summit ridge forms part of the boundary between North Yorkshire and Cumbria, and the famous Ribblehead Viaduct, built for the Settle to Carlisle railway in the 1870s, sits at the foot of the fell.
fun_facts: Whernside is the highest of the Yorkshire Three Peaks
The summit ridge lies on the boundary between North Yorkshire and Cumbria
Ribblehead Viaduct, with its 24 arches, is visible from the ridge
The Settle to Carlisle railway runs through Blea Moor tunnel nearby
Dent and Dentdale lie to the north-east of the fell
walking_guide:
A popular circuit of Whernside starts at Ribblehead, crosses Ribblehead Viaduct, and climbs by Force Gill before following the long summit ridge to the trig point. The descent is by the broad path to Bruntscar, completing a round trip of around eight miles that takes four to five hours. The ridge is exposed to wind, so bring warm clothing, and use a map and compass in poor weather.

Whernside has a long, remote-feeling ridge, and the route from Ribblehead gives a good view of the viaduct and the Settle to Carlisle line. The ridge is windy and exposed, so prepare for conditions several degrees colder than the valley. The Three Peaks Challenge walkers pass through this way, so expect company during summer weekends.

name: Fan Fawr
description: Fan Fawr is in the western Brecon Beacons. The mountain has a distinctive shape and offers good walking with less crowds than Pen y Fan. It rises on the western side of the central Beacons, and the old Roman road of Sarn Helen runs beneath its slopes.
history: Fan Fawr stands on the western side of the central Brecon Beacons and overlooks the A470 and the Storey Arms. It is far quieter than its neighbour Pen y Fan, and it gives a good introduction to the Beacons landscape without the crowds.
fun_facts: Fan Fawr is a Hewitt in the western Brecon Beacons
It is far quieter than Pen y Fan
The Storey Arms lies close to the mountain
The Roman road Sarn Helen runs near its slopes
The summit has views of Pen y Fan and Corn Du
walking_guide:
Fan Fawr is normally climbed from the Storey Arms area, with a path leading across moorland to the summit. The ascent is gentle compared with Pen y Fan, and the walk takes around three hours. The summit has fine views of the Beacons.

The terrain is boggy in places, so wear waterproof boots. Fan Fawr is a good choice for walkers who want a quiet day in the Beacons, or who are looking for a gentler alternative on a busy weekend.

name: Ingleborough
description: Ingleborough has a distinctive flat summit plateau that was once an Iron Age hill fort. It's the second peak in the Yorkshire Three Peaks challenge. Its flat, gritstone-capped summit can be seen for miles and is one of the most recognisable landmarks in the Yorkshire Dales.
history: The summit plateau of Ingleborough carries the remains of an Iron Age hillfort, one of the highest in England, together with a ring of stone walls and hut circles. Below the fell, the limestone country around Ingleton and Clapham is riddled with caves and potholes, including Gaping Gill, one of Britain's best-known underground shafts.
fun_facts: Ingleborough is one of the Yorkshire Three Peaks
The summit plateau holds the remains of an Iron Age hillfort
Gaping Gill, a famous pothole, lies on the fell's southern flank
Ingleborough Cave, near Clapham, is open to visitors as a show cave
The flat top makes the mountain easy to spot from across the Dales
walking_guide:
The most scenic way up Ingleborough starts in Clapham and follows the Ingleborough Estate trail past the cave and Trow Gill before a steady climb to the plateau. Many walkers instead start in Ingleton or at Chapel-le-Dale and climb by the Southerscales path. The final section is a stone-flagged climb onto the flat summit. Allow four to five hours for the round trip and take care in mist, since the plateau is wide and navigation is hard without a map and compass.

Ingleborough is the most varied of the Three Peaks, with caves, potholes and limestone scenery beneath a gritstone summit. The Clapham route is the best choice for visitors who want to see Gaping Gill and Ingleborough Cave, while the shorter Chapel-le-Dale ascent suits walkers short of time. The summit plateau is flat and large, and in cloud it is easy to head in the wrong direction on the descent, so a compass bearing is worthwhile.

name: Ben Stack
description: Ben Stack is an isolated peak with superb views over numerous lochs and to the mountains of Sutherland. The ascent is straightforward but rewarding.

name: Kinder Scout
description: Kinder Scout is the highest point in the Peak District. The plateau is famous for the Mass Trespass of 1932, a pivotal moment in the campaign for access to open country. The high, peaty plateau is the focus of one of the most important moments in British access history.
history: Kinder Scout was the setting of the Mass Trespass of April 1932, when ramblers from Manchester walked onto the plateau in protest at being barred from open moorland. The protest helped lead to the National Parks and Access to the Countryside Act of 1949, and the Peak District became Britain's first national park in 1951.
fun_facts: Kinder Scout is the highest point in the Peak District
The 1932 Mass Trespass took place on the plateau
The Pennine Way begins at Edale, in the Kinder Scout area
Kinder Downfall is a well-known waterfall on the western edge
The plateau is covered in eroded peat groughs
walking_guide:
A classic ascent of Kinder Scout begins at Edale and climbs Grindsbrook Clough onto the plateau, where a path follows the edge to Kinder Downfall before returning by the Pennine Way. The plateau is boggy and featureless, and navigation can be hard in cloud, so a map and compass are essential. Allow five to six hours for the full round trip.

Kinder Scout is a serious moorland plateau, not a gentle hill, and many walkers underestimate the navigation. The peat is deep and sticky after rain, and the Pennine Way path can be badly eroded. A clockwise or anticlockwise edge route is easier to follow than crossing the interior. Edale has a station, a visitor centre and plenty of cafes, which makes it an excellent base for a day on the plateau.

name: Bleaklow
description: Bleaklow is a wild peat moorland plateau. The summit area can be boggy, but the walk offers solitude and great views over the Dark Peak. The plateau has a wild, empty feel, and the wreckage of a wartime aircraft near Higher Shelf Stones is a well-known destination.
history: Bleaklow is the second highest hill in the Peak District, a large plateau of peat that forms part of the Dark Peak. Near Higher Shelf Stones lie the remains of a US Air Force B-29 Superfortress, Over Exposed, which crashed into the moor in November 1948, and the debris can still be seen.
fun_facts: Bleaklow is the second highest hill in the Peak District, after Kinder Scout
The wreckage of the B-29 Superfortress Over Exposed lies near Higher Shelf Stones
The Pennine Way crosses the plateau
The plateau is deep peat, with groughs and bogs
Bleaklow Head is where the Pennine Way crosses the high plateau
walking_guide:
A good route starts in Old Glossop, follows the Doctor's Gate track and the Pennine Way to Bleaklow Head, then visits the B-29 wreckage near Higher Shelf Stones before returning. Allow five to six hours. The paths are clear for much of the route, but the plateau is boggy and the groughs are deep.

Navigation on Bleaklow can be tough in mist, since the ground is open and featureless. It suits walkers who like wild moorland and are comfortable with a compass. Avoid it after heavy rain, and wear waterproof boots.

name: Stac Pollaidh
description: Despite its modest height, Stac Pollaidh is one of Scotland's most distinctive peaks. The sandstone pinnacles and scrambling opportunities make it extremely popular. The red sandstone ridge, topped with pinnacles, gives wide views over Coigach and Assynt and is one of the best short hill walks in the north-west Highlands.
history: Stac Pollaidh, sometimes spelled Stac Polly, is built from Torridonian sandstone sculpted by frost into the towers that crown the summit ridge. It lies in the Coigach area north of Ullapool, in a landscape of isolated peaks including Cul Beag and Suilven.
fun_facts: Stac Pollaidh is built from Torridonian sandstone
The summit ridge is topped with weathered pinnacles
It can be climbed in a couple of hours from the roadside
The view includes Suilven and Cul Beag
It is sometimes spelled Stac Polly
walking_guide:
Stac Pollaidh is climbed from the car park on the single-track road to Achnahaird. A good path rises to a col and then circles the hill, giving a choice of routes onto the ridge. The main summit involves easy scrambling, and the full circuit takes around two to three hours. Be careful on the scrambling sections, particularly in wet or windy weather.

Stac Pollaidh is one of the best short hill days in Scotland, and the circuit takes only a few hours. It is a good choice for a half day when the weather is clear, as the views to Suilven and the sea are excellent. The summit ridge is a real scramble, so take care, and avoid it in strong wind or rain. Midges are common in summer, so bring repellent.

name: Haystacks
description: Despite its modest height, Haystacks was Alfred Wainwright's favorite mountain. His ashes were scattered here, and the summit overlooks Innominate Tarn.

name: Slieve Donard
description: Slieve Donard is the highest peak in Northern Ireland and all of the island of Ireland's east coast, offering spectacular views from Dublin Bay to the Isle of Man on clear days.
history: Named after Saint Domangard, a disciple of St Patrick who reportedly built a chapel on the summit. The Mourne Wall, built between 1904 and 1922, crosses the summit and stretches for 35 kilometres.
fun_facts: Highest peak in Northern Ireland at 850 metres
The Mourne Wall crosses the summit, built entirely by hand
On a clear day you can see Scotland, the Isle of Man, and Dublin Bay
Named after Saint Domangard who built an early Christian oratory on the summit
Part of the Mourne Mountains Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty

name: Slieve Commedagh
description: Slieve Commedagh is the second highest peak in Northern Ireland. The famous Mourne Wall climbs its slopes, and the summit provides outstanding views across the Mournes. The Mourne Wall climbs its slopes and gives walkers an easy way to follow the route in poor visibility.
history: The name means 'mountain of watching' in Irish, likely referring to its use as a lookout point. The Mourne Wall, a remarkable feat of Victorian construction, passes just below the summit.
fun_facts: Second highest peak in Northern Ireland
The Mourne Wall passes over its shoulder
Name means 'mountain of watching' in Irish Gaelic
Often combined with Slieve Donard in a classic ridge walk
Part of the Ulster Way long distance footpath
walking_guide:
The usual route starts in Donard Park in Newcastle, follows the Glen River path to the Saddle between Slieve Donard and Slieve Commedagh, then climbs beside the Mourne Wall to Commedagh. Allow around three to four hours. The path is clear, and the wall is a good guide in mist.

Many walkers combine Commedagh with Slieve Donard to make a longer day. The path from Newcastle is busy at weekends, so start early. The ground on the upper slopes is exposed, so carry waterproofs even in summer.

name: Slieve Binnian
description: Slieve Binnian is one of the most dramatic peaks in the Mournes, famous for its granite tors and 'back castles'. The summit ridge provides some of the finest walking in Northern Ireland.
history: The mountain's distinctive granite tors were sculpted by millennia of weathering. The Silent Valley Reservoir, built in the 1930s to supply Belfast, lies in the valley below.
fun_facts: Famous for dramatic granite tors called the 'back castles'
Overlooks the Silent Valley Reservoir
One of the most photographed mountains in the Mournes
The Mourne Wall crosses its summit
Popular for scrambling on the granite outcrops
facilities: Silent Valley visitor centre and car park

name: Slieve Bearnagh
description: Slieve Bearnagh is known for its distinctive granite tor summits and the Mourne Wall that passes through the col. The mountain offers dramatic rocky scrambling to the twin summits. The Mourne Wall climbs the col beside it, and the granite tors on the summit give a classic Mournes skyline.
history: Slieve Bearnagh is one of the best-known peaks in the Mourne Mountains. The Mourne Wall, built between 1904 and 1922 to enclose the catchment of the Silent Valley and Ben Crom reservoirs, crosses its slopes. The name is often translated as gapped mountain.
fun_facts: Has dramatic twin granite tor summits
The Mourne Wall passes through its col
Excellent scrambling on granite rock
Part of the classic Mourne Wall walk
walking_guide:
A popular route starts at the Trassey Track car park and follows the track to Hare's Gap before climbing beside the Mourne Wall to the col, then onto the summit tors. The round trip takes around four to five hours, and the final scramble onto the tors needs care in wet weather.

The Mournes are rocky and exposed, and weather can change quickly. This route suits walkers who want a classic Mournes day without the long distance of the full Mourne Wall walk. Slieve Bearnagh is also a good choice for photographers because of the tors.

name: The Cobbler
description: The Cobbler, or Ben Arthur, is one of Scotland's most iconic peaks. Although not a Munro, it draws more climbers than many Munros thanks to its spectacular rocky summit and proximity to Glasgow.
history: The three rocky peaks resemble a cobbler at his last, giving the mountain its popular name. The true summit requires a brief scramble through the 'eye of the needle', a hole in the rock.
fun_facts: One of the most popular hills in Scotland despite not being a Munro
The true summit involves scrambling through a hole in the rock called the 'eye of the needle'
Only 90 minutes from Glasgow by train to Arrochar
The three tops resemble a cobbler bending over his last
Classified as a Corbett at 884 metres
national_park: Loch Lomond and The Trossachs National Park

name: Suilven
description: Suilven is perhaps the most iconic silhouette in the Scottish Highlands. Rising dramatically from the Assynt moorland, the mountain's distinctive sugar-loaf profile makes it one of the most photographed peaks in Scotland.
history: The name derives from the Old Norse 'Sul' meaning a pillar. The mountain sits in the heart of Inverpolly Nature Reserve, one of Scotland's most remote and wild landscapes.
fun_facts: Perhaps the most photographed mountain profile in Scotland
Despite its small footprint, has a dramatic profile visible from miles away
Requires a long approach walk of about 8 kilometres through boggy moorland
The summit ridge runs east-west with two distinct tops
Sits in one of Scotland's largest remaining wildernesses

name: Ben Hope
description: Ben Hope is the northernmost Munro in Scotland. It stands in splendid isolation in Sutherland, offering sweeping views to Orkney on clear days. Completing Ben Hope is a significant milestone for Munro baggers.
history: The name derives from the Norse 'hop' meaning a small bay. The mountain stands guard at the head of Loch Hope, and its ascent takes walkers past impressive basalt cliffs.
fun_facts: The northernmost Munro in Scotland
On a clear day you can see the Orkney Islands from the summit
The impressive north face has dramatic basalt cliffs
A significant milestone for Munro baggers completing the northern circuit
The approach from the south passes a remarkable broch, Dun Dornaigil

name: Ben Lui
description: Ben Lui is consistently cited as one of the most beautiful mountains in Scotland. The classic view from Coire Gaothaich shows the steep corrie headwall flanked by twin ridges, creating a near-perfect mountain form.
history: Named from Gaelic meaning 'calf mountain', Ben Lui has long been admired for its elegant shape. The mountain was a favourite of early Scottish mountaineers including W.W. Naismith.
fun_facts: Consistently voted one of the most beautiful mountains in Scotland
The north corrie holds snow well into spring, offering a classic snow climb
Has one of the finest ridge lines in the Southern Highlands
Can be combined with three other Munros on the same day
The Central Gully is a popular winter mountaineering route
facilities: Car park at Dalrigh near Tyndrum
national_park: Loch Lomond and The Trossachs National Park

name: Catbells
description: Catbells is one of the most beloved hills in the Lake District and one of the most climbed in the UK. Despite its modest height, it offers spectacular views over Derwentwater and is perfect for families and beginners. It sits on the western shore of Derwentwater and is a popular choice for families and first-time fell walkers.
history: The name possibly derives from 'Cat Bields', meaning a shelter for wildcats. The fell was immortalised by Beatrix Potter, who set her story of Mrs Tiggy-Winkle on its slopes.
fun_facts: One of the most climbed hills in England
Featured in Beatrix Potter's Mrs Tiggy-Winkle
Provides one of the finest views of Derwentwater in the Lake District
Can be reached by ferry from Keswick
Alfred Wainwright called it 'a family fell' accessible to everyone
walking_guide:
Most walkers climb Catbells from the car park at Hawse End or from Gutherscale, following the clear path up the north ridge. The final section is a short rocky scramble to the summit. A round trip takes around two hours, and many walkers continue to Maiden Moor and High Spy. The path is eroded in places, so wear sturdy footwear.

Catbells is one of the best first fells in the Lakes, and the ascent is short enough to do in a morning. It becomes very busy on summer weekends, so start early or walk in the evening. Combine it with the Keswick Launch for a different way back to town. The final scramble to the summit has some steep rock, which can be slippery in the wet.

name: Pen-y-ghent
description: Pen-y-ghent is the third of the Yorkshire Three Peaks and arguably the most dramatic. The distinctive stepped profile makes it instantly recognisable, and its rocky summit ridge offers an exciting scramble. Its stepped, sloping profile and rocky nose make it the most dramatic of the Yorkshire Three Peaks when seen from Horton in Ribblesdale.
history: The name is thought to derive from Brittonic meaning 'hill of the border territory'. The Three Peaks Challenge, which includes Pen-y-ghent, Ingleborough, and Whernside, began in 1887.
fun_facts: One of the three Yorkshire Three Peaks
Has a distinctive stepped, layered profile
The Three Peaks Challenge was first recorded in 1887
The summit has a stone wind shelter
On the Pennine Way long distance path
walking_guide:
The usual route begins in Horton in Ribblesdale, passes the church, and climbs by Brackenbottom to the foot of the main crag. A short, easy scramble leads to the summit plateau, and the loop can be completed by returning via Hull Pot and Horton Scar Lane. A round trip takes around three to four hours. The scramble sections are easy but can be slippery after rain, so wear boots with a good grip.

Pen-y-ghent is the shortest and most approachable of the Three Peaks, and it is the best choice for walkers who want a taste of Dales scenery in half a day. The scramble is short and straightforward, but the rock is polished and slippery when wet. Horton in Ribblesdale has a cafe and a station, which means the route can be reached by train on the Settle to Carlisle line.

name: Mam Tor
description: Known as the 'Shivering Mountain', Mam Tor is one of the most visited peaks in the Peak District. The famous sunrise views from its summit ridge have made it a magnet for landscape photographers.
history: The summit holds an impressive Iron Age hill fort dating from around 1200 BC. The mountain's nickname 'Shivering Mountain' comes from the frequent landslips on its unstable eastern face, which destroyed the old A625 road.
fun_facts: Known as the 'Shivering Mountain' due to unstable shale rock causing landslips
Has a spectacular Iron Age hill fort on its summit plateau
The old A625 road was repeatedly destroyed by landslips and finally abandoned in 1979
One of the most photographed sunrise locations in England
On the popular Great Ridge Walk connecting to Lose Hill
facilities: National Trust car park at Mam Nick

name: Pen y Ole Wen
description: Pen y Ole Wen is the 'gatekeeper' of the Ogwen Valley, with the steepest direct ascent of any mountain in Wales from Ogwen Cottage. The summit gives stunning views across the Carneddau. From the shore of Llyn Ogwen the climb gains around 650 metres in a short distance, which makes it a serious test for walkers who think the Carneddau are an easy option.
history: The mountain guards the western end of the Carneddau massif. The steep south-west ridge from Ogwen is one of the most challenging routes in Wales, gaining nearly 900 metres in just 2 kilometres.
fun_facts: Has the steepest direct ascent of any mountain in Wales
The 'gatekeeper' of the Ogwen Valley approach to the Carneddau
Often combined with the full Carneddau ridge walk
The summit commands superb views over Snowdonia
Classification as a Hewitt means it has 150m of prominence
walking_guide:
The usual route leaves Ogwen Cottage and climbs steeply up the south-east ridge to the summit. A long and punishing ascent, it can take around two and a half hours for fit walkers, with very little flat ground. The path is clear, but the rocky final section can be slippery. From the summit, the ridge to Carnedd Dafydd is broad and gentler.

The mountain suits walkers who are fit and happy with a steady, strenuous climb. Avoid it in strong winds. Many walkers use Pen y Ole Wen as the start of a longer day over the Carneddau.

name: Moel Hebog
description: Moel Hebog towers above the charming village of Beddgelert and offers one of the finest views of Snowdonia. The mountain is an excellent alternative to the busier Snowdon massif with far fewer crowds.
history: The name means 'hill of the hawk' in Welsh. The mountain was used by Owain Glyndŵr as a hiding place during his uprising against English rule in the early 15th century.
fun_facts: Name means 'hill of the hawk' in Welsh
Owain Glyndŵr reportedly hid in a cave on the mountain
Superb views over the Glaslyn estuary and Cardigan Bay
Often much quieter than nearby Snowdon
Part of a popular circuit with Moel yr Ogof and Moel Lefn

name: Fan y Big
description: Fan y Big is famous for the 'diving board', a flat rock slab that juts out over the escarpment and is one of the most photographed spots in the Brecon Beacons. The views north over the Usk Valley are exceptional.
history: The name means 'peak of the finger' in Welsh. The mountain forms part of the eastern Brecon Beacons and the escarpment along its northern edge is a defining feature of the landscape.
fun_facts: Famous for the 'diving board' rock that juts over the escarpment edge
One of the most photographed spots in the Brecon Beacons
Part of the Brecon Beacons ridge walk from Pen y Fan east
The northern escarpment drops sharply to the Usk Valley
Part of the long Beacons Way footpath
facilities: Car park at Blaen y Glyn

name: Ben Vorlich (Loch Earn)
description: Ben Vorlich above Loch Earn is one of the most popular Munros in the Southern Highlands, offering excellent views for relatively modest effort. Often combined with Stuc a' Chroin.
fun_facts: One of the most popular Munros in the Southern Highlands
Often combined with Stuc a' Chroin for a full day out
Offers superb views of the Southern Highlands and beyond
Accessible from the small village of Ardvorlich on Loch Earn
national_park: Loch Lomond and The Trossachs National Park

name: Cross Fell
description: Cross Fell is the highest point in the Pennines and the highest mountain in England outside the Lake District. The summit is often shrouded in the notorious Helm Wind, the only named wind in England.
history: Previously known as Fiends Fell, it was renamed Cross Fell after St Augustine allegedly erected a cross to drive away demons. The Helm Wind, a fierce north-easterly, is unique to this area.
fun_facts: Highest point in the Pennines
The Helm Wind here is the only named wind in England
Previously called Fiends Fell due to alleged supernatural activity
On the Pennine Way long distance path
The summit plateau is one of the most remote in England

name: Lose Hill
description: Lose Hill is at the eastern end of the Great Ridge in the Peak District. The summit provides panoramic views over Hope Valley and is easily reached from Castleton or Hope village. Together with Mam Tor it forms the Great Ridge, one of the best-known short ridge walks in the Peak District.
history: Lose Hill forms the eastern end of the Great Ridge, which runs west to Mam Tor above the Hope Valley. A memorial viewpoint known as Ward's Piece honours the Sheffield rambling campaigner G. H. B. Ward, who was involved in the fight for access to open moorland.
fun_facts: Eastern end of the Great Ridge walk from Mam Tor
Superb views over Hope Valley and Edale
Popular walking destination near Castleton
Part of the National Trust estate
walking_guide:
Lose Hill is easily climbed from Hope or Castleton. Many walkers follow the Great Ridge from Mam Tor over Back Tor to Lose Hill and descend into Hope. The round trip takes around three hours from Castleton. The paths are clear, and the main hazard is the steep drop on the northern side of the ridge in poor weather.

Lose Hill is one of the best short outings in the Peak District and a good choice for families, beginners and anyone short of time. The Great Ridge is busy at weekends, so start early or walk on a weekday. Combine it with the walk to Mam Tor for a longer day that finishes in Castleton, where there are cafes and pubs.

name: Beinn a Chlachair
description: Beinn a' Chlachair is a remote Munro in the Monadhliath region. It offers superb mountain walking in a wild and quiet area, often visited alongside neighbouring Munros.
fun_facts: One of the more remote Munros in the central Highlands
Often combined with Creag Pitridh and Geal Charn
The name means 'mountain of the mason' in Gaelic

name: Beinn Dorain
description: Beinn Dorain is one of the most striking mountains in Scotland, with a perfect conical shape visible from the main A82 road. The Gaelic poem 'Moladh Beinn Dobhrain' by Duncan Ban MacIntyre immortalised this mountain. The graceful cone is best seen from the A82 near Bridge of Orchy, where the West Highland Way runs beneath it.
history: The mountain inspired Duncan Ban MacIntyre's famous 18th-century Gaelic praise poem. The peak dominates the approach to the Bridge of Orchy and is a familiar landmark to travellers on the West Highland Way.
fun_facts: Inspired one of the greatest Gaelic poems, 'Moladh Beinn Dobhrain'
Has a striking conical shape visible for miles from the A82
Often combined with Beinn an Dothaidh
The West Highland Way passes directly at its foot
One of the most photogenic mountains in the Southern Highlands
facilities: Car park at Bridge of Orchy station
Train station at Bridge of Orchy
national_park: Loch Lomond and The Trossachs National Park
walking_guide:
The usual route starts at the Bridge of Orchy car park, follows the track into Coire an Dothaidh and climbs onto the ridge to Beinn an Dothaidh before continuing to Beinn Dorain. Allow six to seven hours for the full round. The paths are clear, but the upper slopes are steep and rocky, and care is needed in mist.

Bridge of Orchy has a railway station on the West Highland line, so it is easy to reach without a car. This route suits walkers who already have some Munro experience, and the poetic link makes it a good mountain to understand before you go.

name: Beinn Ghlas
description: Beinn Ghlas is one of the Ben Lawers group of Munros, forming part of a ridge that holds many of the highest mountains in the Southern Highlands. The Ben Lawers massif is renowned for its rare arctic-alpine flowers. It is the first summit on the usual path to Ben Lawers, so most walkers cross it without a second thought, but it makes a rewarding objective in its own right.
history: Beinn Ghlas forms the south-western shoulder of the Ben Lawers range above Loch Tay. The mountain is part of the National Nature Reserve managed by the National Trust for Scotland, where the lime-rich rock supports some of the rarest mountain plants in Britain.
fun_facts: Part of the Ben Lawers National Nature Reserve
The Ben Lawers massif holds some of the rarest arctic-alpine plants in Scotland
Often combined with Ben Lawers for a classic two-Munro day
facilities: Car park on the hill road
national_park: Loch Lomond and The Trossachs National Park
walking_guide:
Beinn Ghlas is climbed from the National Trust for Scotland car park on the Ben Lawers road. The path climbs steadily onto the ridge and reaches the summit after a little over two hours for most walkers. From the top a short, clear ridge leads to Ben Lawers itself, so the two Munros are nearly always done together.

If you only want Beinn Ghlas, the round trip is short enough for a half day, which makes it a good choice when the weather closes in higher up. The summit is exposed to the wind, so carry warm layers even in summer.

name: Meall Garbh
description: Meall Garbh is part of the Ben Lawers massif and offers superb views across Loch Tay and the Southern Highlands. It lies beyond An Stùc on the classic ridge walk from Ben Lawers. It is the high point of the eastern end of the Lawers range, reached by the exposed ridge past An Stuc.
history: Meall Garbh is part of the Ben Lawers range above Loch Tay. The ridge that links it with Ben Lawers passes over An Stuc, a rocky and exposed section that makes the full traverse a more demanding day than the standard Ben Lawers route.
fun_facts: Part of the Ben Lawers massif with its rare mountain flora
Can be combined with Ben Lawers and An Stuc for a three-Munro day
national_park: Loch Lomond and The Trossachs National Park
walking_guide:
Meall Garbh is normally climbed along the ridge from Ben Lawers over An Stuc, which involves a scramble and some exposed ground, or from Lawers via Meall Greigh. The ridge is a fine high-level walk, and the full traverse takes around seven to eight hours.

An Stuc has steep, loose rock, and the traverse should be avoided in wet or icy conditions. Walkers who are not happy scrambling can reach Meall Garbh by the easier route over Meall Greigh from the east.

name: Beinn a' Ghlo
description: Beinn a' Ghlo is a massive mountain complex in the central Highlands with three Munro summits. The mountain is a royal shooting estate and offers exceptional wildlife viewing including golden eagles. The three Munros of the massif are linked by a high, undulating ridge, and the highest, Carn nan Gabhar, rises well above its neighbours.
history: Queen Victoria frequently visited Blair Castle nearby and reportedly enjoyed views of Beinn a' Ghlo. The area remains one of the finest grouse moors in Scotland.
fun_facts: Has three Munro summits within its massif
Queen Victoria admired the mountain from Blair Castle
Excellent spot for golden eagle sightings
The name means 'mountain of the veil' in Gaelic
Royal Deeside is visible from the summit on clear days
walking_guide:
The usual route starts at Loch Moraig, near Blair Atholl, and follows a path onto the ridge, taking in the three Munros in turn. Allow eight to ten hours for the full round trip. The paths are clear but the ridge is long and exposed.

The Atholl estate is a working shooting estate, so check stalking restrictions before you go. The mountain is a good choice for walkers who want a high-level day with a fine view of the Cairngorms, but it needs good weather and some stamina.

name: Sgor Gaoith
description: Sgor Gaoith stands on the edge of the Moine Mhòr, the Great Moss, at the rim of the Cairngorm plateau. The summit gives dramatic views down the steep cliffs to Loch Einich. The name is usually translated as peak of the wind, and the airy summit above the cliffs justifies it.
fun_facts: Stands on the edge of dramatic cliffs above Loch Einich
Part of the remote Monadh Mòr group
The views from the summit cliff edge are among the finest in the Cairngorms
facilities: Car park at Loch Einich track
walking_guide:
Sgor Gaoith is usually climbed from Glen Feshie, where a path leads to the high ground and follows the broad ridge to the summit. The final approach to the cliff edge is a spectacular moment, with Loch Einich far below. Allow around six hours for the round trip.

The cliff edge drops steeply, so take care in mist and keep well back in strong winds. This is a good choice for walkers who want views of the Cairngorm plateau without the crowds at Cairn Gorm itself.

name: Beinn Ime
description: Beinn Ime is the highest of the Arrochar Alps and a rewarding Munro accessible from the village of Arrochar. The mountain provides superb views over Loch Long and the Firth of Clyde. It is the highest summit of the Arrochar Alps, a group of steep, rocky hills close to Glasgow.
history: Beinn Ime is the highest of the Arrochar Alps, a compact group of mountains at the head of Loch Long. The nearby Cobbler, or Ben Arthur, is more famous for its rocky summit, but Beinn Ime is the highest of the group and is often climbed together with its neighbour Beinn Narnain.
fun_facts: Highest of the Arrochar Alps
Accessible by train to Arrochar & Tarbet station
Can be combined with The Cobbler for a classic full day
Superb views of the Firth of Clyde
national_park: Loch Lomond and The Trossachs National Park
walking_guide:
Beinn Ime is usually climbed from the car park at Succoth, at the head of Loch Long, and is often combined with Beinn Narnain to make a long day. The ascent is steep and the paths are eroded in places. Allow around six hours for the round trip, and more if you add Beinn Narnain.

The Arrochar Alps are close to Glasgow, so they are busy at weekends. The weather here can be very wet, and the upper slopes are exposed, so carry waterproofs. This is a good choice for walkers who want a proper Munro day within easy reach of the city.

name: Ben Starav
description: Ben Starav is a prominent Munro above the head of Loch Etive with a striking conical shape. The ascent from the River Etive offers dramatic scenery.
fun_facts: Prominent conical peak above Loch Etive
Part of the Glen Etive Munros group
Glen Etive was a filming location for the James Bond film Skyfall
national_park: Loch Lomond and The Trossachs National Park

name: Beinn Fhionnlaidh
description: Beinn Fhionnlaidh is a remote Munro above the western shores of Loch Mullardoch in the Glen Cannich area. It offers wild and remote mountain walking away from the usual tourist routes. Its remoteness is the main challenge, and a walk here is as much about the approach through Glen Cannich as the summit itself.
history: Beinn Fhionnlaidh lies in the Glen Cannich area, close to Loch Mullardoch, a large reservoir created for hydroelectric power. The mountain is far from any road, and the long approach means it sees few visitors compared with the popular Munros further south.
fun_facts: One of the more remote Munros in the Western Highlands
Requires a long approach or a boat across Loch Mullardoch
Part of the Glen Cannich circuit often done as a multi-day trip
walking_guide:
Beinn Fhionnlaidh is a long day, and many walkers use a mountain bike on the estate roads of Glen Cannich to shorten the approach. Allow ten hours or more for the round trip on foot, and plan your route in advance, since paths on the upper ground are faint or absent in places.

This is a mountain for experienced hillwalkers who are happy to navigate without a path. Check the stalking information before you go, because access may be limited during the deer season, and carry spare food, a map and a compass. Tell someone your route before you set off, as mobile signal is unreliable.

name: Cadair Berwyn
description: Cadair Berwyn is the highest point of the Berwyn Mountains, a range of heather moorland hills forming part of the border between England and Wales. The summit provides sweeping views across mid-Wales.
fun_facts: Highest point of the Berwyn Mountains
Part of the border between England and Wales
Remote moorland walking with few other walkers

name: Mynydd Du
description: Mynydd Du, also known as the Black Mountain, is the remote western section of the Brecon Beacons. The high plateau of Bannau Sir Gaer includes the striking glacial lakes of Llyn y Fan Fach and Llyn y Fan Fawr.
history: The area is associated with the legend of the Physicians of Myddfai, a family of physicians descended from a fairy from Llyn y Fan Fach. The legend dates to the 12th century.
fun_facts: The lakes Llyn y Fan Fach and Llyn y Fan Fawr sit below dramatic escarpment cliffs
Associated with the Welsh legend of the Lady of the Lake
Much quieter than the central Brecon Beacons
Part of the Brecon Beacons National Park

name: Plynlimon
description: Plynlimon, or Pumlumon Fawr, is the highest point of central Wales and the source of the rivers Severn and Wye. The boggy summit plateau is part of the Cambrian Mountains.
history: The name Pumlumon means 'five beacons' in Welsh. The rivers Severn (Hafren) and Wye both rise on Plynlimon's slopes within metres of each other, and have been a source of wonder since ancient times.
fun_facts: Source of both the River Severn and River Wye
Highest point of the Cambrian Mountains
The rivers Severn and Wye both rise within metres of each other on its slopes
Name 'Pumlumon' means 'five beacons' in Welsh
Remote moorland walking with excellent views of mid-Wales

name: Pen y Cadair
description: Pen y Cadair is the true summit of Cadair Idris. The mountain is steeped in Welsh mythology — legend says anyone who sleeps on its summit will wake either a poet or a madman. The summit lies above the steep cliffs of Cwm Cau, and the lake of Llyn y Gadair lies in a hollow below the summit ridge.
history: The name means 'chair of Idris', referring to the giant Idris Gawr. Legend states Idris was a giant poet-warrior who used the mountain as his chair to observe the stars. The Minffordd Path is one of the finest routes in Wales.
fun_facts: Legend says sleeping on the summit makes you a poet or a madman
Named after the giant Idris Gawr who used it as a chair
Contains a glacial lake, Llyn y Gadair, in a spectacular corrie
One of the finest ridge walks in southern Snowdonia
The mountain featured heavily in early Welsh Romantic art
walking_guide:
The most popular route, the Minffordd Path, starts from the car park near Tal-y-llyn and climbs past Llyn Cau, one of the finest glacial lakes in Wales, before reaching the summit ridge. The Pony Path, which starts near Dolgellau, is a longer and gentler alternative. Allow five to six hours for either route.

The summit is exposed and can be very windy, and the cliffs of Cwm Cau fall steeply from the ridge, so take care in mist. Cadair Idris is a good choice for walkers who want a full Welsh mountain day with a clear path and varied scenery.

name: Beinn Narnain
description: Beinn Narnain is one of the Arrochar Alps, accessible by train from Glasgow. The summit has fine views towards the Highlands and can be combined with The Cobbler for a satisfying day.
fun_facts: Accessible by train from Glasgow to Arrochar & Tarbet
Part of the popular Arrochar Alps
Can be combined with The Cobbler and Beinn Ime
One of the most accessible Munros from a major city
national_park: Loch Lomond and The Trossachs National Park

name: Beinn Alligin
description: Beinn Alligin is one of the great Torridon mountains, comprising two Munros and one of the most spectacular ridges in Scotland. The Horns of Alligin provide an exhilarating scramble above Loch Torridon. The horseshoe takes in both Munros and crosses the Horns of Alligin, three rocky pinnacles that give a short but airy scramble.
history: The name means 'jewelled mountain' in Gaelic. The mountain's dramatic gash, the Eag Dubh, was created by a massive rock fall thousands of years ago.
fun_facts: Name means 'jewelled mountain' in Gaelic
The Horns of Alligin are classic scrambling pinnacles
Has a dramatic gash called Eag Dubh (Black Cleft) on its side
Part of the magnificent Torridon horseshoe
The Torridon sandstone is some of the oldest rock in Britain at 750 million years old
walking_guide:
The horseshoe starts at the Coire Mhic Nobuil car park, climbs Tom na Gruagaich, crosses to Sgurr Mhor, and returns over the Horns of Alligin. The scramble over the Horns can be bypassed by a path below the pinnacles. Allow six to seven hours. The ridge is exposed, and the descent from the Horns is steep and rocky.

Beinn Alligin is the friendliest of the big Torridon mountains, which makes it the usual first choice for walkers who want a taste of the area without committing to the harder ridges of Liathach or Beinn Eighe. The Horns of Alligin are the crux of the day, and anyone who is nervous about exposure can take the bypass path. Allow time for the long descent back to the glen, and be aware that conditions on sandstone terraces can be very slippery when wet.

name: Beinn Dearg
description: Beinn Dearg is the highest mountain in the north-west Highlands outside the Far North, requiring a long approach through wild country. The remote nature of the approach makes reaching the summit a true adventure. The mountain stands at the centre of a group of high Munros above Loch Broom, and the long approach is part of the reward.
history: Beinn Dearg lies in the wild country south of Ullapool and is the high point of a group of Munros that includes Cona' Mheall, Meall nan Ceapraichean and Eididh nan Clach Geala. The name means red hill, and the mountain is a major landmark in this part of the north-west Highlands.
fun_facts: Highest mountain in the Beinn Dearg group
Requires a long approach of around 10 kilometres
Part of a demanding circuit with Cona' Mheall and Meall nan Ceapraichean
walking_guide:
The usual route starts at Inverlael and follows the track into Gleann na Squaib and on to Coire Granda, climbing to the summit plateau. Allow seven to nine hours for the round trip, and more if you add the neighbouring Munros. The path is good on the lower ground but fades higher up.

The upper slopes are high and exposed, and snow can linger well into spring. This is a challenging day for walkers with some Munro experience, and it is best done in settled weather.

name: Beinn Mhanach
description: Beinn Mhanach is a remote Munro above the head of Loch Lyon. It is one of the more seldom-visited Munros, requiring a long walk-in through Glen Lyon. Its remoteness makes it one of the quieter Munros, and a day here usually means seeing very few other walkers.
history: Beinn Mhanach is a remote Munro above the head of Loch Lyon, in one of the quietest parts of the Southern Highlands. The mountain is usually climbed together with its neighbour Beinn a' Chuirn, and the long approach is a large part of the day.
fun_facts: One of the more remote and less-visited Munros
Accessed via the beautiful and long Glen Lyon
The name means 'monk's mountain' in Gaelic
national_park: Loch Lomond and The Trossachs National Park
walking_guide:
Beinn Mhanach is a long day, and the approach is usually the hardest part. Many walkers use a mountain bike on the estate tracks to save time. Allow eight to ten hours on foot, and check your route carefully before setting off.

This is a mountain for experienced walkers who are comfortable with a long day and some rough ground. Check stalking restrictions before you go, carry a map and compass, and leave details of your plans with someone.

name: Old Man of Storr
description: The Old Man of Storr is the most famous rock pinnacle on the Isle of Skye, though strictly the walk leads to the base of the pinnacle rather than its top. The dramatic needles and pillars are one of the most photographed landscapes in Scotland.
history: Geological landslips created these extraordinary formations from the Trotternish Ridge. The rock was first climbed in 1955 by Don Whillans. The area features in numerous films and television productions.
fun_facts: One of the most photographed landscapes in Scotland
The pinnacle was first climbed in 1955 by Don Whillans
The surrounding area is used as a filming location including for Prometheus
The formations are the result of massive landslips on the Trotternish Ridge
One of Skye's most visited attractions

name: The Quiraing
description: The Quiraing is a remarkable series of pinnacles, rock towers, and hidden plateaux on the northern Trotternish Ridge on Skye. The walk through this extraordinary landscape is one of the finest in Scotland.
history: The Quiraing was formed by a massive landslip of basalt lava flows. The hidden table at the heart of the Quiraing was reportedly used by locals to hide cattle from Viking raiders.
fun_facts: One of the most extraordinary landscapes in Britain
The hidden 'Table' was used to hide cattle from Viking raiders
Created by the largest ongoing landslip in the UK
Featured in films and television including Stardust and Outlander
The car park regularly has queues of cars in summer
facilities: Car park on the Staffin to Uig road

name: Lingmell
description: Lingmell is a magnificent fell above Wasdale with superb views of the Scafell massif and Mosedale. Often overshadowed by its famous neighbours, the summit provides some of the best views in the Lake District.
fun_facts: Superb viewpoint for the Scafell massif
Part of the classic Wasdale ridge circuit
Often overlooked despite its excellent position

name: Kidsty Pike
description: Kidsty Pike is the highest point on the popular Coast to Coast walk at the point where it descends to Haweswater. Its distinctive sharp pike is visible from miles around.
fun_facts: Highest point on Alfred Wainwright's famous Coast to Coast walk
The pointed summit is distinctive and easily recognised
Overlooks Haweswater Reservoir

name: Catstycam
description: Catstycam is a shapely pyramid peak beside Helvellyn, reached via the exciting Swirral Edge arête. The mountain gives exceptional views over Red Tarn and Helvellyn.
fun_facts: A shapely pyramid peak beside Helvellyn
Reached via the exciting Swirral Edge arête
The summit gives exceptional views over Red Tarn

name: Foel Fras
description: Foel Fras is the most northerly of the Carneddau Hewitts and provides a natural end to the magnificent Carneddau ridge walk. The views north over Anglesey and the Irish Sea are excellent.
fun_facts: Most northerly Hewitt in the Carneddau range
Natural end to the full Carneddau ridge walk
Views extend to Anglesey and Ireland on clear days
facilities: Car park at Bwlch y Ddeufaen

name: Pen yr Helgi Du
description: Pen yr Helgi Du is a superb outlier of the Carneddau range with a distinctive ridge leading from Pen y Gwryd. The mountain provides excellent views over Snowdonia and the Conwy Valley.
fun_facts: A striking outlier of the Carneddau range
The narrow east ridge makes for exciting ridge walking
Can be combined with Pen Llithrig y Wrach
restaurants: Tyn y Coed Inn, Capel Curig

name: Moelwyn Mawr
description: Moelwyn Mawr is the highest of the Moelwyn group of mountains between Blaenau Ffestiniog and Porthmadog. The summit gives wonderful views across the bay towards the Llŷn Peninsula.
fun_facts: Highest of the Moelwyn group
Superb views over the Glaslyn estuary
Crossed by the Ffestiniog Railway corridor below

name: Red Pike (Buttermere)
description: Red Pike above Buttermere is one of the finest Lake District summits, with a dramatic red rocky peak giving sensational views over Buttermere and Crummock Water. The descent via Scale Force, England's highest waterfall, is outstanding.
fun_facts: The distinctive red colour comes from iron-rich rocks
Scale Force, England's highest waterfall, is nearby
Superb views over Buttermere and Crummock Water

name: Thornthwaite Crag
description: Thornthwaite Crag is a shapely summit topped with a tall stone beacon column, one of the most distinctive landmarks in the Lake District. The fell forms part of the High Street horseshoe. The tall stone column on the summit is visible for miles around, and the view along the Kentmere and Troutbeck valleys is one of the best in the eastern fells.
history: Thornthwaite Crag stands on the ridge above the Troutbeck and Kentmere valleys, close to the line of the Roman road known as High Street. The tall stone beacon on its summit, one of the landmarks of the eastern fells, is a tall stone column built by shepherds.
fun_facts: Topped by a striking tall stone beacon visible from miles away
Part of the High Street horseshoe ridge walk
Offers panoramic views over the Troutbeck and Kentmere valleys
walking_guide:
Thornthwaite Crag is normally climbed from Troutbeck or Hartsop, with the path following the old Roman road along the ridge. The ascent is steady and the summit is reached after about two hours. A longer round of the Kentmere Horseshoe passes over the summit.

The ridge is exposed, so carry a windproof layer even on a fine day. The beacon is a useful landmark in mist, but be careful of the steep slopes on the western side.

name: Sgurr na Banachdich
description: Sgurr na Banachdich is one of the Cuillin Ridge Munros on Skye, the most technically demanding mountain range in Britain. The peak provides extraordinary views over the Cuillin horseshoe. It is often regarded as one of the more approachable Cuillin Munros, but the scrambling near the summit still demands care.
fun_facts: One of the few 'relatively' accessible Cuillin Munros
The Cuillin Ridge is the hardest mountain terrain in Britain
Requires basic scrambling to reach the summit safely
facilities: Car park and campsite at Glenbrittle
walking_guide:
The usual route starts at Glen Brittle and climbs into Coire na Banachdich before scrambling up to the ridge and the summit. The scrambling is straightforward for experienced hill walkers, but steep rock and loose scree require care. Allow around six hours for the round trip.

The Cuillin are rough and rocky and the weather is changeable, so choose a clear day. Mist makes route finding hard in the corrie, and the gabbro rock can affect compasses near the ridge. This is a good choice for walkers who want a taste of the Cuillin without committing to the most serious scrambles.

name: Beinn Mheadhoin
description: Beinn Mheadhoin is a high Cairngorm Munro with a distinctive and unusual summit of rounded granite tors. The mountain sits at the heart of the Cairngorm plateau.
fun_facts: Has distinctive rounded granite tors on its summit
Sits at the heart of the Cairngorm plateau
Can be reached from Cairn Gorm car park on a long day

name: Beinn Bhrotain
description: Beinn Bhrotain is a high Munro on the edge of the Moine Mhòr, the Great Moss of the Cairngorms. It is a remote mountain that rewards those willing to make the long approach. It is one of the remotest Munros in the Cairngorms, and a day here usually combines a long walk-in with a quiet summit.
fun_facts: Sits on the edge of the Great Moss (Moine Mhòr)
One of the higher remote Cairngorm summits
The approach from Glen Dee is through exceptional wilderness
facilities: Car park at Linn of Dee
walking_guide:
Beinn Bhrotain is usually climbed from the Linn of Dee car park, near Braemar. Many walkers cycle along the track to White Bridge to save time, then walk up Glen Geusachan to reach the mountain, often combining it with neighbouring Monadh Mor. Allow ten hours or more for the round trip.

This is a big day in remote country with no phone signal. Take a map, a compass and spare layers, and be prepared for the weather to change quickly on the plateau. Check the deer stalking season before planning a visit.

name: Sgurr nan Coireachan
description: Sgurr nan Coireachan above Glenfinnan has one of the most romantic settings in Scotland. The Glenfinnan Viaduct and monument to Bonnie Prince Charlie lie in the valley below. The mountain rises above Glenfinnan, where the viaduct and the monument to the Jacobite rising of 1745 attract visitors from around the world.
history: Bonnie Prince Charlie's standard was raised at Glenfinnan in 1745 to begin the Jacobite uprising, visible from the mountain's ridge. The iconic Glenfinnan Viaduct, now famous from the Harry Potter films, is prominent in the valley.
fun_facts: The Glenfinnan Viaduct (famous from Harry Potter) is visible from the ridge
Bonnie Prince Charlie raised his standard at Glenfinnan below
Part of a remote Munro circuit in the Rough Bounds of Knoydart
Exceptionally remote and wild approach
walking_guide:
Sgurr nan Coireachan is normally climbed from Glenfinnan, often together with Sgurr Thuilm to make a long day. The route follows tracks and paths into the hills before climbing to the ridge. Allow seven to nine hours for the round trip.

The weather on the west coast is changeable, and the ridge can be exposed. Take a map and compass, and check the route on a current guide, as paths may be faint in places.

name: Conwy Mountain
description: Conwy Mountain is a small but dramatic ridge above the medieval walled town of Conwy. Despite its modest height, the coastal views over the Conwy Estuary and towards Anglesey are outstanding.
history: The summit holds an ancient Iron Age hill fort, Castell Caer Seion, one of the best preserved in Wales. The walls of the fortification are still clearly visible and form part of the walking route.
fun_facts: Has an Iron Age hill fort on the summit
Views over the medieval town of Conwy and its castle
One of the most accessible hills in North Wales
Part of the North Wales Path long distance route
